_comment: Behaviour rules injected into the security agent's system prompt at runtime.
This file exists so that teaching the agent about a new threat is a CONFIG
edit, not a model fine-tune. Editing a quantized GGUF is not possible, and
even a LoRA on the base model would need a GPU, thousands of labelled
examples, and a re-quantize step for every change. Rules here take effect on
the next classification -- no rebuild, no restart, no retraining.
It is read on every classification if the file's mtime changed, so an
operator can tune wording on a live box and see the effect immediately.
IMPORTANT: rules shape JUDGEMENT, not DETECTION. Counting '4 distinct
operations in 5 minutes' is a deterministic job and belongs in SQL (see
sql_scripts/7610_ransomware_sequence.sql). What the model adds is deciding
whether a matched sequence is an attack or the nightly archive job that
always does exactly those four things.

always_alert._comment: Statement classes where precedent is NOT a defence. Mirrors fingerprint.PRIVILEGED_SHAPES; the agent short-circuits these before the model is even called.
always_alert.text: Precedent NEVER excuses an inherently privileged action. GRANT, REVOKE, DROP, ALTER, CREATE, TRUNCATE, BACKUP and RESTORE stay SECURITY_ALERT even if seen before -- 'it happened yesterday too' is not an argument that it is safe.

threats.name: Ransomware / destructive-sequence behaviour
threats.text: RANSOMWARE SHAPE: a short burst of DISTINCT destructive operations by one login is the signature, not any single statement. Mass UPDATE of many rows, mass DELETE, dropping or truncating tables, disabling auditing or logging, deleting backups, and reading large volumes of data -- four or more different such operations within a few minutes, from the same login, is a strong ransomware indicator EVEN IF each individual statement has precedent on this server. Scheduled archive and ETL jobs produce a similar shape, so weigh whether the login, program and hour match a routine schedule. Say explicitly in the reason which operations formed the chain.

threats.name: SQL injection
threats.text: INJECTION SHAPE: tautologies (OR 1=1), stacked statements after a semicolon, UNION SELECT grafted onto an application query, comment truncation (-- or /*), or string concatenation building a WHERE clause. These are alerts regardless of precedent, because an application that has been injected once will show the injected shape as 'precedent' thereafter.

threats.name: Bulk data exfiltration
threats.text: EXFILTRATION SHAPE: SELECT of credential, payment or PII columns without a narrow WHERE clause; SELECT INTO OUTFILE / OPENROWSET / BULK operations; or a query returning far more rows than the same statement shape normally does on this server.

threats.name: Privilege and schema enumeration
threats.text: RECONNAISSANCE SHAPE: sweeping the catalog -- sys.databases, information_schema, sys.server_principals, fn_my_permissions, xp_cmdshell probing, sp_configure reads. One such query is routine for a DBA tool; a sequence of them from an application login is not.

threats.name: Authentication (356 detections)
threats.text: Authentication (356 detections), e.g. No MFA enforcement; Multi-tenancy needs; Expired certificates; Incomplete migration; Performance concerns.

threats.name: Authorization (237 detections)
threats.text: Authorization (237 detections), e.g. Role Assignment Errors; Inadequate Role Testing; Performance Assumptions; Fear of Breaking Changes; Shared Database Accounts.

benign_hints._comment: Guidance that keeps the agent from crying wolf. Kept separate so it is obvious what makes the agent QUIETER, and reviewable as a group.
benign_hints.text: Backup, index-maintenance and statistics jobs run destructive-looking statements on a schedule. If the login, program name and hour match a recurring pattern in the precedent, say so -- but note that matching a schedule is not by itself sufficient when the statement class is privileged.

DBDOME's own collector queries read the catalog constantly. Statements selecting from sys.dm_exec_*, sys.dm_os_* or information_schema with no writes, from the monitoring login, are the product observing itself.

custom._comment: Site-specific rules go here. Add freely; each becomes a bullet in the prompt.
custom.name: example - not used
custom.text: Set enabled=true and edit the text. Keep each rule to one paragraph: a small model follows a short, concrete instruction far better than a long one.

SEC-ANL-PII-001-RC01.name: Sensitive data observed in dbanalytics catalog views
SEC-ANL-PII-001-RC01.desc: The DBDOME dbanalytics catalog stores observed query text from monitored targets in monitoring.v_expensive_queries and monitoring.v_active_transactions. If queries on monitored servers reference PII columns (SSN, credit card, password, email, salary, etc.), the data leaks into these aggregation views and becomes visible to anyone with read access to the dbanalytics catalog. This RC scans both views for sensitive patterns so leaks can be triaged and the upstream queries hardened or masked.

SEC-SQL-PRI-006-RC01.name: Public role has SELECT on PII tables
SEC-SQL-PRI-006-RC01.desc: Tables with sensitive columns are accessible to the public/PUBLIC role — meaning every authenticated principal can read them.

SEC-SQL-PRI-008-RC02.name: Backups not encrypted
SEC-SQL-PRI-008-RC02.desc: Most recent backups are stored without encryption. PPL Reg §15 requires backup encryption for High-level databases.

SEC-SQL-PRI-008-RC03.name: Backups stored on same volume as data files
SEC-SQL-PRI-008-RC03.desc: Backup files reside on the same physical volume as the live database files — defeats the purpose of backup as disaster recovery.

SEC-SQL-PRI-009-RC01.name: Records older than retention threshold in PII tables
SEC-SQL-PRI-009-RC01.desc: Tables containing personal data hold rows older than 7 years (default retention threshold). PPL §14 requires deletion when no longer needed for the registered purpose.

SEC-SQL-PRI-009-RC02.name: Inactive subjects with persistent personal data
SEC-SQL-PRI-009-RC02.desc: Customer / user records with no recorded activity for >5 years still hold full personal data — should be archived or anonymised.

SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC07.desc: Devices with old passwords causing repeated lockouts

SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC08.name: Application-layer lockout not implemented
SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC08.desc: Database has no native lockout, application doesn't compensate

SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC09.name: Progressive delay not configured as alternative
SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC09.desc: More sophisticated throttling mechanisms not implemented instead of hard lockout

SEC-DOC-AUD-003-RC08.name: Timestamp Skew
SEC-DOC-AUD-003-RC08.desc: Server clocks are unsynchronized, causing cleanup scripts to delete "future" or "old" logs incorrectly.

SEC-DOC-AUD-006-RC02.name: Granularity Level
SEC-DOC-AUD-006-RC02.desc: The audit level is set to "Statement" instead of "Row," failing to capture *which specific patient record* was accessed (HIPAA violation).

SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC10.name: Manual unlock process too cumbersome
SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC10.desc: Organizations avoid lockouts because unlocking requires administrator intervention

SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC11.name: No differentiation between user types
SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC11.desc: Same lockout policy (or lack thereof) for admin accounts and regular users

SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC12.name: Account lockout conflicts with availability requirements
SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC12.desc: High-availability systems cannot tolerate any service disruption from lockouts

SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC13.name: Scheduled task accounts not monitored
SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC13.desc: Batch jobs with wrong credentials exhaust lockout threshold

SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC14.name: Mobile device credential caching
SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC14.desc: Phones/tablets reconnecting with expired passwords trigger lockouts

SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC15.name: Terminal session persistence
SEC-DOC-AUTH-009-RC15.desc: Disconnected sessions maintaining old credentials causing ongoing failures

SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC02.name: No absolute timeout configured
SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC02.desc: Only idle timeout set, allowing sessions to remain active indefinitely with periodic activity

SEC-DOC-AUD-006-RC03.name: Timezone Confusion
SEC-DOC-AUD-006-RC03.desc: Logs are recorded in local server time instead of UTC, making cross-system correlation impossible for forensic timelines.

SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC03.name: User experience prioritized over security
SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC03.desc: Business requirements to minimize re-authentication leads to long timeouts

SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC04.name: No session timeout policy defined
SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC04.desc: Organization lacks standards for session duration across systems

SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC05.name: Client-side timeout enforcement
SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC05.desc: Session expiration handled by client, which can be manipulated or bypassed

SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC04.name: Driver/SDK default settings
SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC04.desc: Some database drivers don't validate certificates by default, requiring explicit enabling

SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC06.name: No session renewal/rotation
SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC06.desc: Session IDs never refreshed, increasing hijacking window

SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC07.name: Different timeouts across authentication methods
SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC07.desc: Cookie auth has long timeout while API tokens have short timeout, creating confusion

SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC08.name: Legacy application compatibility
SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC08.desc: Older applications break with short timeouts, preventing security improvements

SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC09.name: High-privilege accounts using same timeout as regular users
SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC09.desc: Admin sessions persist as long as regular user sessions

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC03.name: Role-Level Over-Provisioning Instead of User-Level
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC03.desc: Permissions granted at team or department level rather than individual user basis, causing unnecessary access proliferation across entire groups.

SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC10.name: WebSocket/persistent connection handling
SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC10.desc: Long-lived connections bypass session timeout mechanisms

SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC11.name: Server-side session store not implemented
SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC11.desc: Client-side cookies track sessions without server validation

SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC05.name: Self-signed certificate accommodation
SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC05.desc: Validation disabled to allow self-signed certificates instead of properly trusting them

SEC-DOC-AUD-004-RC01.name: File Permissions (777)
SEC-DOC-AUD-004-RC01.desc: Audit log files are created with world-readable/writable permissions (`chmod 777`) on the filesystem.

SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC12.name: No distinction between idle and absolute timeout
SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC12.desc: Single timeout value insufficient for security and usability balance

SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC13.name: Session timeout not enforced at database level
SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC13.desc: Application manages sessions, database accepts any valid credential without time checking

SEC-SQL-PRI-009-RC03.name: Soft-deleted rows never purged
SEC-SQL-PRI-009-RC03.desc: Tables with is_deleted / deleted_at flags retain rows for >2 years after soft-deletion. Soft delete is not deletion under PPL §14.

SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC14.name: Remember me functionality overrides timeout
SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC14.desc: Persistent login features extend sessions far beyond security policy

SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC15.name: Mobile app sessions never expire
SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC15.desc: Native applications maintain permanent sessions for convenience

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC02.name: Lack of Access Review Process
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC02.desc: No periodic audit of assigned permissions; users retain elevated privileges from previous roles even after job transitions without formal deprovisioning.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC05.name: Insufficient Understanding of Role Semantics
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC05.desc: Administrators assign roles without fully understanding the complete set of operations each role permits, assuming roles are narrower than they actually are.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC16.name: Backup and Restore Processes
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC16.desc: Backup/restore utilities require admin credentials; those same credentials sometimes reused for application access.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC06.name: Migration Shortcuts and Temporary Solutions Becoming Permanent
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC06.desc: Initial temporary elevated access for migration projects never revoked; workarounds for permission issues resolved by granting higher privileges instead of fixing root cause.

SEC-DOC-AUD-004-RC02.name: Shared Volume
SEC-DOC-AUD-004-RC02.desc: Audit logs are stored on the same disk partition as the database data files; an attacker with database shell access can wipe both.

SEC-DOC-AUD-004-RC03.name: Missing File Integrity Monitoring (FIM)
SEC-DOC-AUD-004-RC03.desc: No agent is installed to alert when an audit log file is modified or deleted.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC09.name: Custom Roles Not Properly Scoped
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC09.desc: User-defined roles created with overly broad collections, databases, or action sets rather than restricting to specific resources needed.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC10.name: Lack of Separation of Duties (SoD) Enforcement
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC10.desc: Single users granted permissions for both creating and approving operations, or for conflicting critical functions without requiring multiple actors.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC11.name: Insufficient Documentation of Permission Purpose
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC11.desc: Permissions assigned without documented business justification, making it difficult to validate necessity or identify excess.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC12.name: No Automated Privilege Analysis
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC12.desc: Manual role assignment without tools to calculate and compare actual data access patterns versus granted permissions, preventing identification of over-privileging.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC13.name: Complexity of Nested Role Hierarchies
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC13.desc: Deep role hierarchies with multiple levels of inheritance make it difficult to understand full effective permissions of assigned roles.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC14.name: Legacy System Integration Requiring Broad Access
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC14.desc: Integrations between old and new systems requiring higher privileges at database level than modern architectures would necessitate.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC03.name: Flat User Model Without Roles
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC03.desc: Systems using simple user credentials (username/password) without role assignment framework; everyone gets identical access regardless of actual job function.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC04.name: All Users in Admin/Member Category
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC04.desc: In systems like CouchDB with binary admin/member model, all users assigned to "members" role with equivalent permissions due to lack of custom role support.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC05.name: Documentation Gaps on RBAC Setup
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC05.desc: RBAC implementation is optional and requires configuration; insufficient documentation or awareness leads organizations to skip this step entirely.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC06.name: Legacy Authentication-Only Design
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC06.desc: RBAC retrofitted to old databases designed primarily for authentication; organizations unaware RBAC exists as separate layer to configure.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC07.name: Simple Credentials in Development Carrying to Production
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC07.desc: Single shared credentials used in development environment; no RBAC structure ever created because team expects simple access model to scale.

SEC-DOC-AUD-004-RC04.name: Root/Admin Shared Access
SEC-DOC-AUD-004-RC04.desc: Database administrators share the `root` or `sudo` password for the underlying OS, giving them the ability to scrub traces of their actions.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC08.name: Separation of Concerns Not Implemented
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC08.desc: Different applications, environments, or tenants sharing single database without role isolation; treating database as single-user or single-application resource.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC09.name: Misconfiguration During Initial Setup
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC09.desc: Database deployed with authentication enabled but no users/roles defined; single default user created without role assignment structure.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC10.name: Missing Formal Access Control Policy
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC10.desc: No organizational policy requiring RBAC implementation; security governance does not mandate role-based control for databases.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC11.name: Over-Simplification of Permission Model
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC11.desc: Assumption that firewall/network isolation and connection-level authentication are sufficient; database-level RBAC deemed unnecessary overhead.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC12.name: No Role Definition Process
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC12.desc: Organizations lack formal process to define roles based on job functions before deploying database; cannot create roles without predefined template or methodology.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC13.name: Insufficient IAM/RBAC Tooling
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC13.desc: No centralized identity management system; manual role assignment too cumbersome without automated tools, leading to abandonment of RBAC initiative.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC14.name: Multi-Tenancy Without Role Isolation
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC14.desc: Multiple customers/departments sharing instance; no role structure created because each user granted equivalent access without fine-grained differentiation.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC01.name: Insufficient Granularity Understanding
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC01.desc: Administrators unaware that database engines support multi-level access control (database → collection → document); treat database as atomic unit.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC13.name: Scope Creep in Role Definitions
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC13.desc: Roles initially defined narrowly expanded over time to resolve "permission denied" errors rather than creating new narrower roles.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC15.name: Migration Projects Using Admin Access
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC15.desc: Data migration tools or scripts use admin credentials for convenience; artifacts persist in version control or deployment pipelines.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC02.name: Default to Highest-Available Granularity
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC02.desc: For simplicity, permission grants made at database level to avoid complexity; not progressively narrowed to minimum necessary scope.

SEC-DOC-AUD-006-RC05.name: Application User Masking
SEC-DOC-AUD-006-RC05.desc: The application connects using a shared service account; the database audit log sees "svc_webapp" for every transaction, failing to identify the actual human user (GDPR accountability gap).

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC03.name: Tooling Limitations or Unfamiliarity
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC03.desc: UI/CLI tools for granular permission assignment unclear or poorly documented; administrators default to coarser-grained database-level permissions.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC04.name: Role Incompatibility with Collection-Level Access
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC04.desc: Using pre-built database roles not designed for collection-level control; custom role creation requires elevated effort not undertaken.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC05.name: Database Schema Design Not Considering Access Control
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC05.desc: Collections created for logical organization, not security boundaries; no attempt to align collection structure with access control requirements.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC06.name: Multi-Application Sharing Single Database
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC06.desc: Multiple applications/teams sharing same database without collection-level isolation; broad database access granted rather than restricting per collection.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC07.name: Legacy Database Structure
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC07.desc: Databases migrated from relational systems with one-user model; collection-level access control never designed into schema.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC08.name: Performance Assumptions
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC08.desc: Incorrect belief that collection-level permissions have higher overhead; database-wide permissions granted believing they're more efficient.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC09.name: Over-Privileged Platform Teams
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC09.desc: Infrastructure/platform team granted database-wide admin access; application teams inherit overly broad permissions without partition.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC10.name: Lack of Access Control Planning
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC10.desc: Database schema designed for functional requirements only; access control requirements and boundaries not defined during design phase.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC11.name: Inadequate Role Testing
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC11.desc: Role assignments tested only against happy-path scenarios; collection-level restrictions not validated to ensure narrowness.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC12.name: Evolution of Permission Requirements
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC12.desc: Initial narrow collection-level permissions later broadened to database-level during project iterations; never narrowed back.

SEC-DOC-AUD-006-RC04.name: Missing Metadata
SEC-DOC-AUD-006-RC04.desc: The log format (e.g., basic text) captures the query but lacks context like `sessionID`, `clientIP`, or `sslProtocol`.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC14.name: Missing Inventory of Data Sensitivity
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC14.desc: No classification of collections by sensitivity level; cannot align coarse-grained vs fine-grained permissions with data classification.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC15.name: Shared Collections for Multiple Purposes
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-003-RC15.desc: Single collection used for multiple data types or business contexts; cannot restrict access per data type without artificial partitioning.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC01.name: Permissions Not Properly Validated
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC01.desc: Access control lists or role definitions created but not validated to ensure they actually prevent unauthorized access in practice.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC02.name: Default Deny Not Implemented
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC02.desc: Systems allowing implicit access when not explicitly denied; "allow if not forbidden" model instead of "deny if not explicitly allowed."

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC03.name: Wildcard or Overly Broad Permission Patterns
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC03.desc: Permissions defined using wildcards (e.g., `*`, `collection.*`, `items/*`) permitting access far broader than intended.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC11.name: Service Account Best Practices Not Followed
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC11.desc: Applications not assigned individual service accounts; shared admin account used across multiple applications.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC04.name: Role Assignment Errors
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC04.desc: Users assigned incorrect roles due to manual process failures; wrong role IDs referenced or duplicate assignment to higher-privilege roles.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC05.name: Lack of Access Control Validation Testing
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC05.desc: No test suite validating that users can only access intended resources; "happy path" only tested during QA.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC06.name: rootcause or Default Credentials
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC06.desc: Default credentials used for multiple users/applications; anyone with default password gets access intended for specific user.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC07.name: Cross-Database Permission Leakage
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC07.desc: Permissions on one database inadvertently granting access to other databases (e.g., inheritance from admin database).

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC08.name: Implicit Role Inheritance Misconceptions
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC08.desc: Administrators not understanding that roles inherit permissions from parent roles; users given more access than apparent from direct role assignment.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC09.name: Time-Based Access Not Implemented
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC09.desc: Temporary access granted for short-term tasks never revoked; permissions become permanent despite intended expiration.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC10.name: No Active Directory/LDAP Synchronization
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC10.desc: User directories getting out of sync; users retain database access after being removed from organizational directory.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC11.name: API/SDK Defaults Override Role Restrictions
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC11.desc: Application code using higher-privilege defaults or root credentials despite users having lower-privilege roles assigned.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC12.name: Shared Database Accounts
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC12.desc: Multiple users sharing single database account; individual authorization impossible, all users get same access.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC13.name: Query-Level or Document-Level Access Control Missing
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC13.desc: Role grants access to entire collection; users can query or modify any document despite authorization requirements at document level.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC14.name: Insufficient Access Boundary Testing
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC14.desc: Permissions tested within authorized context but not tested with unauthorized attempts (cross-user, cross-collection access attempts).

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC15.name: Collection-Level Access Control Not Fully Enforced
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC15.desc: System allows collection-level role definition but implementation gaps permit cross-collection access through alternative APIs or query patterns.

SEC-DOC-AUD-004-RC05.name: Lack of Remote Shipping
SEC-DOC-AUD-004-RC05.desc: Logs exist only locally on the server; if the server is compromised, the evidence is destroyed.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC16.name: Privilege Escalation Paths Exist
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC16.desc: Users can modify their own roles, access unprotected admin collections, or exploit misconfigurations to escalate privileges.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC17.name: Default Admin Paths Not Restricted
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC17.desc: Built-in admin collections, databases, or system resources not restricted despite user-level RBAC on other resources.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC18.name: Missing Encryption at Rest
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-004-RC18.desc: Even if access controls correct, copied database files or backups accessible without authorization.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC02.name: Permission Errors During Development
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC02.desc: Developers encounter "access denied" errors during initial testing; rather than configuring proper permissions, elevated credentials used to bypass issues.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC03.name: "It Works" Deployment Mentality
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC03.desc: Application working with admin credentials in development deployed to production unchanged; credential transition deferred and never executed.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC04.name: Lack of Application-Level Privilege Separation
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC04.desc: No distinction between privileged operations (schema changes, user management) and data operations (CRUD); all operations use single admin connection.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC05.name: Monolithic Application Design
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC05.desc: Single application layer with all functions combined; cannot separate admin operations from data access without major refactoring.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC06.name: Over-Provisioning for Simplicity
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC06.desc: Admin credentials provisioned for "in case we need it"; becomes default for all connections to avoid troubleshooting specific permission issues.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC07.name: Credentials Stored Insecurely
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC07.desc: Admin credentials hardcoded in code, config files, or environment variables; must be changed infrequently due to difficulty of updates across all deployments.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC08.name: Fear of Breaking Changes
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC08.desc: After initial production deployment, administrators reluctant to change credentials or roles due to risk of downtime; admin credentials remain for perceived stability.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC09.name: Multi-Purpose Database Access
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC09.desc: Single database connection string used for multiple purposes (schema migrations, backups, application data access); all must work with admin privileges.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC10.name: No Privilege Requirement Analysis
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC10.desc: Application never audited to determine actual required privileges; assumed to need all permissions available.

SEC-DOC-AUD-004-RC06.name: Non-WORM Storage
SEC-DOC-AUD-004-RC06.desc: The S3 bucket or Azure Blob container destination does not have "Object Lock" or Write-Once-Read-Many policies enabled.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC12.name: Lack of Connection String Management
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC12.desc: Credentials embedded in application deployment packages or configuration files without separation of privilege levels.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC13.name: No Application-Level Role Enforcement
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC13.desc: Application's business logic not enforcing additional authorization; relies entirely on database credentials for all access control.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC14.name: Temporary Access for Troubleshooting Becomes Permanent
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC14.desc: Admin credentials provisioned for debugging production issues; never revoked after troubleshooting completed.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC17.name: No Difference Between Development and Production Credentials
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC17.desc: Same database user/password used across environments; admin credentials necessary for dev/test remain used in production.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC18.name: Third-Party Tool Integration
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC18.desc: External tools (BI, reporting, analytics) requiring elevated access provisioned with admin credentials; applications connected to same database then use same account.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC01.name: Audit Logging Disabled by Default
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC01.desc: Database audit features not enabled during initial deployment; organizations unaware of logging capabilities or choose not to enable due to performance concerns.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC02.name: No Audit Retention Policy
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC02.desc: Audit logs enabled but not retained; logs rotated and deleted after default period without long-term storage policy.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC03.name: Audit Logs Not Centralized
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC03.desc: Each database node maintains separate audit logs; no aggregation across cluster making it difficult to correlate events or track complete picture.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC04.name: Insufficient Audit Scope
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC04.desc: Audit logging enabled but not capturing permission-related events; may only log data access, not role/permission modifications.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC05.name: Unreadable or Unstructured Log Format
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC05.desc: Audit output in unstructured format or binary; no tooling to parse, correlate, or alert on permission change events.

SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC09.name: Resource constraints
SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC09.desc: Insufficient IT security staff or time to properly configure all database instances

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC06.name: Audit Data Not Indexed or Searchable
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC06.desc: Logs captured but stored in non-queryable format (unstructured files); cannot efficiently search for specific permission changes.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC07.name: No Real-Time Alerting on Permission Changes
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC07.desc: Audit logs generated but not monitored; unauthorized permission changes detected only during manual audits, weeks or months later.

SEC-DOC-NET-001-RC04.name: rootcause Subnet Deployment
SEC-DOC-NET-001-RC04.desc: The database instance was deployed into a rootcause Subnet with an auto-assigned rootcause IP address.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC08.name: Audit Logs Excluded from Backup/Recovery Processes
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC08.desc: Audit logs not backed up; lost during database failures or not recovered during restore operations.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC09.name: Insufficient Audit Event Details
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC09.desc: Logs capture "user modified" but lack contextual information (who performed modification, when, what specifically changed, from what to what).

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC10.name: Manual Permission Management Without Change Tracking
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC10.desc: Permission modifications performed directly without change management process; no audit trail of justification or approval.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC11.name: No Integration with SIEM/Security Tools
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC11.desc: Audit logs generated but not shipped to centralized security monitoring; isolated from other security event streams.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC12.name: Audit Configuration Not Version-Controlled
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC12.desc: Audit settings not documented; changes to audit logging configuration itself not tracked, audit scope may be inadvertently reduced.

SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC06.name: Application framework defaults
SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC06.desc: Web frameworks or ORMs with insecure default TLS verification settings

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC13.name: Access to Audit Logs Not Restricted
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC13.desc: Anyone can delete or modify audit logs; audit trail not immutable, can be altered by bad actors to cover tracks.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC14.name: Insufficient Audit History for Forensics
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC14.desc: Audit logs retained only for compliance period (e.g., 90 days); not available for long-term forensic analysis if breach discovered later.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC15.name: No Differentiation Between Approved vs Unauthorized Changes
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC15.desc: Audit logs capture all changes without indication of whether changes were approved through change control process.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC16.name: Audit Event Categories Not Defined
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC16.desc: No clear categorization of what constitutes permission change event; low-level database events captured instead of high-level authorization events.

SEC-DOC-AUD-004-RC07.name: Plaintext Storage
SEC-DOC-AUD-004-RC07.desc: Logs containing sensitive query data are stored unencrypted, allowing any user with disk access to read them.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC17.name: No Human-Readable Reasons/Justification Captured
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC17.desc: Audit entry does not capture business justification or ticket/change request number; difficult to validate legitimacy of changes.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC18.name: Audit Logs Not Monitored During Incidents
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC18.desc: Audit logs exist but not actively monitored; permission modifications during security incidents not noticed until post-breach analysis.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC19.name: Performance Impact of Auditing Not Managed
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC19.desc: Comprehensive auditing creates performance overhead; disabled to improve performance without considering security trade-offs.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC20.name: No Compliance Requirement Driving Audit Implementation
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-006-RC20.desc: Without regulatory requirement (HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOX), audit logging not prioritized; treated as optional feature.

SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC02.name: Development/testing configurations promoted to production
SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC02.desc: Non-encrypted configurations used in dev/staging environments are mistakenly deployed to production without security hardening

SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC03.name: Performance concerns
SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC03.desc: Teams disable TLS believing it causes unacceptable latency or throughput degradation without proper testing

SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC04.name: Legacy application compatibility
SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC04.desc: Older applications or drivers may not support TLS connections, and teams prioritize functionality over security

SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC05.name: Lack of awareness of security requirements
SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC05.desc: Database administrators or developers don't understand the criticality of encrypting data in transit

SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC06.name: Missing or inadequate security policies
SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC06.desc: Organization lacks formal policies mandating encryption in transit for database connections

SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC07.name: Complexity of TLS configuration
SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC07.desc: Perceived difficulty in configuring certificates, key files, and connection strings leads to avoidance

SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC08.name: Quick deployment pressure
SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC08.desc: Rush to get systems operational leads to skipping security configuration steps

SEC-DOC-AUD-005-RC01.name: Double-Switch Requirement
SEC-DOC-AUD-005-RC01.desc: The admin enabled auditing in the database parameter group but missed the second step of enabling "CloudWatch Logs Export" in the cluster modification screen.

SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC10.name: Miscommunication between teams
SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC10.desc: Security teams assume TLS is enabled while database teams assume it's not required

SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC11.name: Documentation gaps
SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC11.desc: Inadequate internal documentation on how to enable TLS for specific database engines

SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC12.name: Third-party vendor requirements
SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC12.desc: External applications or services connecting to the database don't support encrypted connections

SEC-SQL-PRI-010-RC01.name: Failed-login spike from a single source
SEC-SQL-PRI-010-RC01.desc: >20 failed login attempts from the same host / login in the last 60 minutes — possible credential-stuffing or brute-force attack.

SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC13.name: Monitoring/alerting gaps
SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC13.desc: No automated checks to verify TLS is enabled on all database instances

SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC14.name: Configuration management drift
SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC14.desc: TLS settings disabled during troubleshooting and never re-enabled

SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC02.name: Default cipher suite acceptance
SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC02.desc: Database accepts whatever cipher suites are offered without restricting to strong modern algorithms

SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC03.name: Insufficient knowledge of cipher suite security
SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC03.desc: Administrators don't understand differences between secure and insecure cipher suites

SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC04.name: Configuration complexity
SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC04.desc: Difficulty understanding how to specify minimum TLS versions and allowed cipher suites in database configuration

SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC05.name: Incomplete security scanning
SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC05.desc: Vulnerability scanners report weak TLS but findings are not acted upon or prioritized

SEC-DOC-NET-001-RC02.name: Default Security Group
SEC-DOC-NET-001-RC02.desc: In AWS/Azure, creating a "default" security group often allows all traffic to ease initial connectivity testing.

SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC06.name: Compliance requirement misunderstanding
SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC06.desc: Teams believe meeting minimum compliance standards (e.g., "must use TLS") is sufficient without understanding version requirements

SEC-DOC-NET-001-RC05.name: Load Balancer Misconfig
SEC-DOC-NET-001-RC05.desc: The database is behind a Load Balancer that is internet-facing, bridging the gap to the private database.

SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC07.name: Testing environment leakage
SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC07.desc: Weak ciphers enabled for testing older client compatibility never removed from production

SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC08.name: Driver/client library limitations
SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC08.desc: Older database drivers don't support TLS 1.2+ or modern cipher suites, forcing downgrade

SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC09.name: Lack of centralized TLS policy enforcement
SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC09.desc: No organization-wide standard for minimum TLS versions and cipher suites

SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC10.name: Copy-paste configuration errors
SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC10.desc: Administrators copy outdated configuration examples from old documentation or forums

SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC11.name: Performance optimization misconceptions
SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC11.desc: Belief that older TLS versions or simpler cipher suites perform better

SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC12.name: Vendor/partner requirements
SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC12.desc: Third-party integrations explicitly require support for older TLS versions

SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC13.name: Gradual deprecation delays
SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC13.desc: Organizations plan to upgrade TLS but repeatedly postpone due to perceived risk or complexity

SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC14.name: Audit finding remediation backlog
SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC14.desc: Weak TLS identified in audit but remediation delayed due to resource constraints or competing priorities

SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC02.name: Feature only available in enterprise/paid editions
SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC02.desc: Cost considerations lead organizations to forgo paid editions with encryption features

SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC09.name: Weekend/holiday expiration
SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC09.desc: Certificates expire during off-hours with no one monitoring

SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC03.name: Performance impact concerns
SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC03.desc: Perception or reality that encryption at rest significantly degrades database performance

SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC04.name: Complexity of key management
SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC04.desc: Teams lack infrastructure or expertise to properly manage encryption keys

SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC05.name: Cannot be enabled on existing databases
SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC05.desc: Encryption at rest must be configured at database/cluster creation time, making retrofitting difficult

SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC06.name: Lack of regulatory compliance pressure
SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC06.desc: Organizations not subject to regulations requiring encryption at rest don't prioritize implementation

SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC05.name: Application architecture incompatibility
SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC05.desc: Legacy applications not designed for field-level encryption can't be easily retrofitted

SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC07.name: False sense of security from other controls
SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC07.desc: Reliance on perimeter security, disk encryption, or physical security as alternatives

SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC08.name: Initial development decisions persist
SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC08.desc: Database created without encryption during PoC or development, never migrated to encrypted version

SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC09.name: Migration complexity and downtime
SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC09.desc: Enabling encryption requires data migration with associated downtime and risk

SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC10.name: Insufficient security architecture review
SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC10.desc: Database implementation lacks security team involvement during design phase

SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC11.name: Missing data classification
SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC11.desc: Organization hasn't identified which databases contain sensitive data requiring encryption at rest

SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC12.name: Budget constraints
SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC12.desc: Encryption features require premium licensing or KMS services with associated costs

SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC13.name: Vendor lock-in concerns
SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC13.desc: Enabling cloud provider encryption features creates dependencies on specific platforms

SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC14.name: Legacy system constraints
SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC14.desc: Older database versions don't support encryption at rest, and upgrade path is complex

SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC15.name: Lack of automated compliance checking
SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC15.desc: No tools scanning for unencrypted databases across the organization

SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC01.name: Complexity of implementation
SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC01.desc: Client-Side Field-Level Encryption (CSFLE) requires significant application code changes

SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC02.name: Limited query capabilities
SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC02.desc: Encrypted fields have restricted query operations (typically only equality), limiting application functionality

SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC03.name: Only available in Enterprise editions
SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC03.desc: Automatic encryption not available in community/free versions, requiring manual explicit encryption

SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC04.name: Key management infrastructure gaps
SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC04.desc: Requires external KMS integration (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault) that may not exist

SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC06.name: Performance concerns
SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC06.desc: Field-level encryption adds latency to read/write operations and indexing overhead

SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC07.name: Developer knowledge gaps
SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC07.desc: Development teams lack expertise in implementing CSFLE or queryable encryption

SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC08.name: Data model limitations
SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC08.desc: Cannot encrypt certain field types (arrays, nested documents) or special fields like _id

SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC09.name: Operational complexity
SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC09.desc: Managing encryption schemas, data key rotation, and multiple client configurations increases operational burden

SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC10.name: Cost-benefit analysis
SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC10.desc: Organizations question whether PII in specific fields warrants the implementation effort

SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC11.name: Lack of clear data classification
SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC11.desc: Teams don't know which specific fields contain sensitive data requiring field-level encryption

SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC12.name: Testing and QA challenges
SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC12.desc: Encrypted data complicates testing, debugging, and data validation processes

SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC13.name: Backup and disaster recovery complications
SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC13.desc: Field-level encrypted data requires maintaining key access for recovery scenarios

SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC14.name: Integration with existing applications
SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC14.desc: Middleware, reporting tools, and analytics platforms may not support encrypted fields

SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC15.name: Documentation and example gaps
SEC-DOC-ENC-004-RC15.desc: Limited vendor documentation on real-world implementation patterns beyond basic examples

SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC02.name: Manual certificate tracking processes
SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC02.desc: Spreadsheet-based or ad-hoc tracking that falls out of date

SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC03.name: Decentralized certificate management
SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC03.desc: Different teams managing certificates without central visibility

SEC-DOC-AUD-005-RC02.name: IAM Permission Errors
SEC-DOC-AUD-005-RC02.desc: The database service role lacks the `logs:CreateLogGroup` or `logs:PutLogEvents` permission needed to push to CloudWatch.

SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC04.name: Forgotten or undocumented certificates
SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC04.desc: Certificates installed and never added to inventory

SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC05.name: Notification fatigue
SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC05.desc: Certificate expiry warnings ignored or not routed to correct teams

SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC06.name: Renewal process delays
SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC06.desc: Bureaucratic procurement or approval processes prevent timely renewal

SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC07.name: Testing environment certificates in production
SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC07.desc: Short-lived test certificates mistakenly deployed to production

SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC08.name: Multi-cluster deployment oversight
SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC08.desc: Certificate renewed on some database nodes but not all in a cluster

SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC10.name: Lack of certificate ownership
SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC10.desc: Unclear responsibility for which team/person renews database certificates

SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC11.name: Renewal complexity
SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC11.desc: Complicated process requiring multiple approvals or vendor interactions discourages proactive renewal

SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC12.name: Calendar/task management failures
SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC12.desc: Manual reminders not set or ignored in busy operational environments

SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC13.name: Third-party CA dependencies
SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC13.desc: Delays in obtaining renewed certificates from external certificate authorities

SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC14.name: Intermediate certificate chain expiration
SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC14.desc: Focus on leaf certificate expiry while intermediate CA certificates expire

SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC15.name: Lack of automation
SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC15.desc: No automated certificate renewal using ACME or similar protocols

SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC01.name: Development/test certificates promoted to production
SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC01.desc: Self-signed certificates created for local testing never replaced with CA-signed certificates

SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC02.name: Cost avoidance
SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC02.desc: Organizations avoid paying for CA-signed certificates even for internal production systems

SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC03.name: Speed of deployment priority
SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC03.desc: Generating self-signed certificate is faster than going through CA issuance process

SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC04.name: Internal-only system misconception
SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC04.desc: Belief that internal systems don't need CA-signed certificates

SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC05.name: Lack of internal PKI infrastructure
SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC05.desc: No internal certificate authority for issuing production certificates

SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC06.name: Technical knowledge gaps
SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC06.desc: Administrators don't understand how to obtain and install CA-signed certificates

SEC-DOC-NET-001-RC03.name: Debugging access
SEC-DOC-NET-001-RC03.desc: A developer temporarily opened port 27017/8091 to the rootcause internet to debug a connection issue and forgot to close it.

SEC-DOC-NET-001-RC06.name: Docker Port Mapping
SEC-DOC-NET-001-RC06.desc: Running a container with `-p 27017:27017` usually binds to all interfaces (0.0.0.0) on the host by default, bypassing host firewall rules (Docker modifies iptables directly).

SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC07.name: Certificate procurement process barriers
SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC07.desc: Complex approval or purchasing processes discourage proper certificate acquisition

SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC08.name: "It works" mentality
SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC08.desc: Self-signed certificates provide encryption, so security requirement perceived as met

SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC09.name: Missing security policy enforcement
SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC09.desc: No organizational policy prohibiting self-signed certificates in production

SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC10.name: Emergency troubleshooting remnants
SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC10.desc: Self-signed certificate created during outage troubleshooting never replaced

SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC11.name: Lack of certificate inventory visibility
SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC11.desc: Organizations don't know which systems are using self-signed certificates

SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC12.name: Free certificate options unknown
SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC12.desc: Teams unaware of free CA options like Let's Encrypt for certain use cases

SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC13.name: Shadow IT deployments
SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC13.desc: Database instances deployed without formal approval or security review

SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC14.name: Compliance blindness
SEC-DOC-ENC-006-RC14.desc: No regular audits checking certificate types across infrastructure

SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC11.name: Lack of security code review
SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC11.desc: Certificate validation bypass in application code not caught during review

SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC01.name: Manual key rotation processes
SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC01.desc: Keys not rotated due to complexity and operational risk of rotation procedures

SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC02.name: Lack of centralized key management system
SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC02.desc: Keys stored in configuration files, environment variables, or ad-hoc locations

SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC12.name: Missing security testing
SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC12.desc: No automated security tests checking that certificate validation is enabled

SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC03.name: Insufficient key rotation frequency
SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC03.desc: No defined policy for how often encryption keys should be rotated

SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC04.name: No automated key rotation capability
SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC04.desc: Lack of tools or processes to automate key rotation without downtime

SEC-SQL-PRI-010-RC02.name: Privilege escalation event detected
SEC-SQL-PRI-010-RC02.desc: Recent ALTER / GRANT events that elevated a non-admin login to sysadmin / superuser / db_owner.

SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC05.name: Keys stored insecurely
SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC05.desc: Encryption keys in plaintext configuration files, source code repositories, or unencrypted storage

SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC06.name: Lack of key versioning
SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC06.desc: No system to track which data was encrypted with which key version

SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC07.name: Missing key backup and recovery procedures
SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC07.desc: No documented process for key backup or disaster recovery

SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC08.name: Hardcoded keys in application code
SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC08.desc: Encryption keys embedded in source code or configuration checked into version control

SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC09.name: Same key used across multiple environments
SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC09.desc: Production and development databases using identical encryption keys

SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC10.name: No separation of duties
SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC10.desc: Same administrators with access to keys and encrypted data

SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC11.name: Lack of key access auditing
SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC11.desc: No logging of who accesses or uses encryption keys

SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC12.name: Key management platform complexity
SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC12.desc: Enterprise KMS solutions too complex for teams to adopt effectively

SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC13.name: Downtime requirements for key rotation
SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC13.desc: Key rotation requires database downtime, preventing regular rotation

SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC14.name: Cost of external KMS services
SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC14.desc: Organizations avoid cloud KMS services due to cost concerns

SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC15.name: Regulatory compliance gaps
SEC-DOC-ENC-007-RC15.desc: No formal key management policy meeting compliance requirements (FIPS 140-2, PCI-DSS)

SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC01.name: Development testing configurations in production
SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC01.desc: `tlsAllowInvalidCertificates` or similar flags enabled for testing never removed

SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC07.name: Documentation examples copied blindly
SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC07.desc: Tutorials showing certificate validation bypass for simplicity copied to production code

SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC08.name: Complexity of proper certificate trust
SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC08.desc: Administrators don't understand how to properly configure certificate trust stores

SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC09.name: "It's internal network" false security
SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC09.desc: Belief that internal database connections don't need certificate validation

SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC10.name: Legacy compatibility requirements
SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC10.desc: Older database versions or drivers with limited certificate validation support

SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC13.name: Certificate chain issues
SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC13.desc: Incomplete intermediate certificate chains lead to validation bypass instead of fixing chain

SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC14.name: Load balancer TLS termination confusion
SEC-DOC-ENC-008-RC14.desc: Application thinks load balancer validates certificates, disables client validation

SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC03.name: Performance Optimization
SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC03.desc: Administrators intentionally disabled logging to reduce I/O latency or CPU overhead during a high-traffic event and failed to re-enable it.

SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC04.name: Configuration File Errors
SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC04.desc: Syntax errors in the configuration file (e.g., `mongod.conf`, `local.ini`) caused the auditing subsystem to fail to start, falling back to a disabled state.

SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC05.name: Feature Flag Oversight
SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC05.desc: In cloud environments, the "Audit" feature flag or parameter group setting (e.g., DocumentDB `audit_logs`) was left at the default `disabled`/`none` setting.

SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC06.name: Missing Output Destination
SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC06.desc: The audit destination (file, syslog, console) was not specified or the path provided is invalid/unwritable by the database service user.

SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC07.name: Service Restart Pending
SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC07.desc: Configuration changes to enable auditing were made but the database service was not restarted to apply them.

SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC08.name: License Expiration
SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC08.desc: An Enterprise license expired, causing the database to revert to features that do not support auditing.

SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC09.name: Container/Image Defaults
SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC09.desc: Docker images or Helm charts used for deployment were pulled from a repository that defaults auditing to "off" and were not overridden.

SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC10.name: Storage Volume Issues
SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC10.desc: The partition dedicated to logs became full, causing the database to stop writing audit logs or disable the collector to prevent a crash.

SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC11.name: Logging Level Mismatch
SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC11.desc: The logging level is set effectively to "Off" or "Fatal" only, filtering out all standard audit events.

SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC01.name: Default Filter Too Narrow
SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC01.desc: The default audit filter only captures administrative actions (DDL) and ignores data access (DML) or authentication events.

SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC02.name: Syntax Error in Filter
SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC02.desc: A regex or JSON error in the audit filter string caused the database to ignore the custom rule and fall back to a minimal default.

SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC03.name: Role Exclusions
SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC03.desc: The audit policy was configured to exclude "System" or "Admin" users to reduce noise, creating a blind spot for privileged insider threats.

SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC04.name: Missing "Success" Events
SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC04.desc: Configuration only logs "Failed" login attempts (to spot brute force) but fails to log "Successful" logins (needed for forensics).

SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC05.name: New Command Gaps
SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC05.desc: The database was upgraded, introducing new command types (e.g., new aggregation stages) that are not covered by the existing legacy audit filter.

SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC06.name: Read vs. Write Focus
SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC06.desc: Auditing is enabled for "Write" operations only, leaving "Read" (data exfiltration) invisible.

SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC07.name: Local vs. Remote/LDAP
SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC07.desc: Auditing is configured to track local database users but fails to capture identity metadata for users authenticating via LDAP/Kerberos/OIDC.

SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC08.name: API Surface Area
SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC08.desc: Auditing tracks operations via the standard port (e.g., 27017) but misses operations performed via side-channels like the legacy HTTP console or REST API.

SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC09.name: Sampling is Active
SEC-DOC-AUD-002-RC09.desc: To save space, the system is configured to log only a random sample (e.g., 10%) of events, guaranteeing gaps.

SEC-DOC-NET-001-RC07.name: Legacy "Allow All"
SEC-DOC-NET-001-RC07.desc: An old firewall rule `ALLOW ALL` was migrated from an on-prem intranet environment to the cloud without modification.

SEC-DOC-NET-002-RC02.name: Dynamic IPs
SEC-DOC-NET-002-RC02.desc: The server receives a dynamic IP via DHCP; the admin uses `0.0.0.0` because hardcoding the dynamic IP causes the service to fail on reboot.

SEC-DOC-NET-002-RC03.name: Multi-Interface Confusion
SEC-DOC-NET-002-RC03.desc: The server has a management interface and a data interface; the admin binds to "all" to ensure it works on both without understanding the risk.

SEC-DOC-NET-002-RC04.name: Copy-Paste Tutorials
SEC-DOC-NET-002-RC04.desc: Many online tutorials (StackOverflow, blogs) instruct users to "set bind_ip to 0.0.0.0" as step \#1 to fix connection errors.

SEC-DOC-NET-002-RC05.name: IPv6 Complexity
SEC-DOC-NET-002-RC05.desc: Confusion about how to bind specific IPv6 addresses leads users to use the wildcard `::/0` or `[::]`.

SEC-DOC-NET-003-RC01.name: CIDR Math Errors
SEC-DOC-NET-003-RC01.desc: An admin intends to allow a single IP (e.g., `1.2.3.4/32`) but accidentally allows a massive range (e.g., `1.2.3.4/0` or `1.2.0.0/16`).

SEC-DOC-NET-003-RC02.name: App Server Range
SEC-DOC-NET-003-RC02.desc: The database allows the entire subnet of application servers (e.g., `/24`) rather than the specific security group of the apps.

SEC-DOC-NET-003-RC03.name: Temporary Rules Permanent
SEC-DOC-NET-003-RC03.desc: A rule labeled "Temp access for vendor" is created but never deleted.

SEC-DOC-NET-003-RC04.name: Service Port Ranges
SEC-DOC-NET-003-RC04.desc: Opening a wide range of ports (e.g., 8000-9000) because the documentation was unclear about which specific ports were needed.

SEC-DOC-NET-003-RC05.name: "Trusted" Zones
SEC-DOC-NET-003-RC05.desc: A policy that allows "Any Traffic from Corporate HQ" assumes the HQ network is secure, ignoring insider threats or compromised workstations.

SEC-DOC-NET-004-RC01.name: Legacy Classic Mode
SEC-DOC-NET-004-RC01.desc: The deployment was created in an older cloud account (e.g., EC2-Classic) that predates mandatory VPC usage.

SEC-DOC-NET-004-RC02.name: PaaS defaults
SEC-DOC-NET-004-RC02.desc: Some Database-as-a-Service (DBaaS) offerings default to a "rootcause Endpoint" model for ease of onboarding (e.g., Atlas free tier) unless "Peering" is explicitly configured.

SEC-DOC-NET-004-RC03.name: Connectivity Complexity
SEC-DOC-NET-004-RC03.desc: Setting up VPC Peering or Transit Gateways between the Application VPC and Database VPC was deemed too complex.

SEC-DOC-NET-004-RC04.name: External Integrations
SEC-DOC-NET-004-RC04.desc: The database needs to be accessed by a 3rd party SaaS tool (e.g., BI tool) that doesn't support VPN/Private Link, forcing a rootcause deployment.

SEC-DOC-NET-004-RC05.name: Cost
SEC-DOC-NET-004-RC05.desc: Private endpoints or VPC peering can incur data processing charges that rootcause internet traffic sometimes avoids (depending on the provider).

SEC-DOC-NET-005-RC01.name: Feature Cost
SEC-DOC-NET-005-RC01.desc: "Private Link" or "Private Endpoint" features often carry an additional hourly cost per endpoint.

SEC-DOC-NET-005-RC02.name: DNS Complexity
SEC-DOC-NET-005-RC02.desc: Private Endpoints require correctly configured private DNS zones to resolve the hostname to the private IP; misconfiguration here leads users to fallback to rootcause IPs.

SEC-DOC-NET-005-RC03.name: Transitive Routing Limits
SEC-DOC-NET-005-RC03.desc: Private Endpoints often don't support transitive routing (e.g., VPN -> VPC A -> VPC B -> Endpoint), leading users to bypass them.

SEC-DOC-NET-005-RC04.name: Availability
SEC-DOC-NET-005-RC04.desc: The specific region or availability zone does not support the Private Endpoint service for that database engine.

SEC-DOC-NET-005-RC05.name: Migration Inertia
SEC-DOC-NET-005-RC05.desc: The database was set up using rootcause endpoints (with IP filters) before Private Link was available, and re-architecting is low priority.

SEC-DOC-NET-006-RC01.name: Flat Network Topology
SEC-DOC-NET-006-RC01.desc: The organization uses a single "Production" VPC/Network where Web Servers, App Servers, and Databases all reside on the same subnet.

SEC-DOC-NET-006-RC02.name: Hardcoded IPs
SEC-DOC-NET-006-RC02.desc: Applications rely on hardcoded IP addresses, making it difficult to move the database to a segregated secure subnet.

SEC-DOC-NET-006-RC03.name: Container Networking
SEC-DOC-NET-006-RC03.desc: In Kubernetes, all pods (Apps and DBs) are running in the same namespace without Network Policies defined to restrict traffic.

SEC-DOC-NET-006-RC04.name: Database as Queue
SEC-DOC-NET-006-RC04.desc: The database is being used as a message queue between microservices, requiring broad connectivity from many different network segments.

SEC-DOC-NET-006-RC05.name: Management Access
SEC-DOC-NET-006-RC05.desc: Admins put the database in the "Management" subnet to make it easier to SSH into, breaking segmentation from the "Data" plane.

SEC-DOC-INJ-001-RC01.name: Direct concatenation of user input into queries
SEC-DOC-INJ-001-RC01.desc: Developers building queries by string concatenation rather than using parameterized approaches

SEC-DOC-INJ-001-RC02.name: Absence of input sanitization libraries
SEC-DOC-INJ-001-RC02.desc: Not using tools like mongo-sanitize, express-mongo-sanitize, or similar validation frameworks

SEC-DOC-INJ-001-RC03.name: Lack of type validation
SEC-DOC-INJ-001-RC03.desc: Accepting generic object types (map[string]interface{}, interface{}) instead of strongly-typed structs

SEC-DOC-INJ-001-RC04.name: Missing schema validation
SEC-DOC-INJ-001-RC04.desc: No enforcement of expected data types and structures at application layer

SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC01.name: Aerospike default admin creds
SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC01.desc: Admin user created at installation with hardcoded username `admin` and password `admin`; not randomized per deployment.

SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC08.name: No password complexity enforcement
SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC08.desc: Databases allow any character sequence; no minimum entropy check at password set time.

SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC09.name: Shared credentials across team
SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC09.desc: Single password given to entire development/operations team, reducing accountability and increasing exposure surface.

SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC01.name: Default configuration not overridden
SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC01.desc: Database deployed with factory defaults that disable authentication to reduce setup friction and operational complexity for initial deployments.

SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC02.name: Protected-mode misconfiguration (Redis specific)
SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC02.desc: Redis `protected-mode` enabled but `requirepass` not set, providing false sense of security while only blocking non-localhost connections; administrators assume protection exists when it only applies locally.

SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC15.name: No password complexity rules in documentation
SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC15.desc: Setup guides omit password requirements; admins follow path of least resistance.

SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC03.name: Memcached architecture design
SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC03.desc: Memcached fundamentally lacks native authentication mechanisms; designed exclusively for trusted network environments; assumes deployment behind firewalls with application-level only access.

SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC04.name: SASL not compiled/enabled (Memcached)
SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC04.desc: Memcached SASL support not built at compile time (`--enable-sasl` flag omitted); even when available, SASL flag (`-S`) not passed during service startup.

SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC05.name: etcd RBAC disabled by default
SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC05.desc: etcd deliberately ships with authentication disabled by design decision to lower friction for new users; documented behavior since project inception in 2013.

SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC06.name: DynamoDB security group misconfiguration
SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC06.desc: AWS security groups allow all inbound traffic (0.0.0.0/0) instead of restricting to application subnets; combined with IAM bypass enables unauthenticated access.

SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC07.name: Docker/container default exposures
SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC07.desc: Containerized deployments (Redis, Memcached, Aerospike) run without authentication flags in docker-compose or Kubernetes manifests; `ENTRYPOINT` or `CMD` does not include authentication parameters.

SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC08.name: Infrastructure-as-code templates reuse
SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC08.desc: Copy-paste of deployment templates from examples, quick-start guides, or PoCs lacking authentication into production without security configuration step.

SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC09.name: Development environment promoted to production
SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC09.desc: Temporary development instances with disabled authentication never hardened before production deployment; configuration drift allowed authentication to remain disabled.

SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC10.name: Service restart without persistence
SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC10.desc: Servers restarted after updates or incidents lose authentication settings if configured only in memory via runtime commands (`CONFIG SET`, `CONFIG REWRITE` not executed).

SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC11.name: Bind address set to 0.0.0.0
SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC11.desc: Redis, Aerospike, or etcd explicitly bound to all interfaces (0.0.0.0 or ::) to enable remote access for legitimate reasons, but without concurrent authentication enablement.

SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC12.name: Microservices network trust assumptions
SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC12.desc: Internal Kubernetes clusters, corporate networks, or VPCs assumed to be "trusted" so authentication deemed unnecessary; perimeter security relied upon exclusively.

SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC13.name: Rapid scaling without security review
SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC13.desc: Auto-scaling deployments spin up new instances from unsigned AMIs, container images, or Terraform modules that lack authentication configuration.

SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC14.name: Authentication feature disabled for troubleshooting
SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC14.desc: Administrator temporarily disables authentication (`CONFIG SET requirepass ""`, `redis-cli CONFIG REWRITE`, or `etcdctl auth disable`) to diagnose issues and forgets to re-enable.

SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC15.name: Third-party managed service misconfiguration
SEC-KV-AUTH-001-RC15.desc: Hosted Redis/Memcached/DynamoDB services accessed without enabling provider-specific authentication (ElastiCache auth token, DynamoDB IAM, Aerospike cloud credentials).

SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC01.name: Dictionary passwords selected
SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC01.desc: Administrators choose common words, names, or simple patterns (password123, admin, redis, mydb) susceptible to dictionary attacks.

SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC02.name: Insufficient password length
SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC02.desc: Passwords shorter than 12-16 characters used due to operational convenience; easier to type and remember but weak against brute force.

SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC03.name: Low character complexity
SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC03.desc: Passwords lack uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and special characters; rely on single character class increasing entropy insufficiently.

SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC04.name: Default passwords never changed
SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC04.desc: Aerospike default `admin:admin`, Memcached/Redis initialization user passwords, or cloud-generated temporary passwords left unchanged in production.

SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC05.name: Password reuse across environments
SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC05.desc: Same weak password deployed across dev, staging, and production reducing apparent risk (in dev context) but endangering production.

SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC06.name: Weak hashing algorithm or no salt
SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC06.desc: Even if strong password, poor storage mechanisms (SHA256 without salt/iterations) make cracking feasible; Aerospike/Memcached may store plaintext or use weak algorithms.

SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC07.name: Passwords derived from predictable data
SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC07.desc: Passwords based on organization name, domain, hostname, or current date making them guessable from open-source intelligence.

SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC10.name: Password hardcoded in scripts/configs
SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC10.desc: Weak passwords chosen specifically because they fit easily in shell scripts, CI/CD configs, or application code; stronger passwords would break shell quoting.

SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC11.name: Manual password generation without cryptographic randomness
SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC11.desc: Administrators create passwords manually (1-2-3-4-5, qwerty, asdf) instead of using `openssl rand`, `base64`, or password generators.

SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC12.name: Environmental variables expose weak patterns
SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC12.desc: Passwords stored in .env files or Kubernetes secrets follow predictable naming (DB_PASSWORD=password, REDIS_AUTH=redis123).

SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC13.name: Weak password policy not enforced by database
SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC13.desc: Databases accept weak passwords because no validation at set-time; Redis `requirepass` accepts any string.

SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC14.name: Password rotation never implemented
SEC-KV-AUTH-002-RC14.desc: Weak password set once and never changed; attackers with old password maintain access indefinitely.

SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC02.name: Temporary credentials left in place
SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC02.desc: Cloud provider generates temporary password at provisioning (DynamoDB, ElastiCache); not rotated before application deployment.

SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC03.name: Deployment automation skips credential rotation
SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC03.desc: Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, or deployment scripts do not include step to change default credentials post-provisioning.

SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC04.name: Documentation examples use defaults
SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC04.desc: Setup guides show configurations with default creds as examples; copied verbatim without changes.

SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC05.name: Known-credential exploitation
SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC05.desc: rootcause lists of default credentials (Shodan, CVE databases) include Aerospike admin:admin, Redis default, etc.; attackers scan for these.

SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC06.name: No credential change verification step
SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC06.desc: Deployment checklist or monitoring does not verify that defaults were changed; humans assume it was done.

SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC07.name: Service principal/IAM role uses defaults
SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC07.desc: AWS IAM role or service account created with default policies; not scoped to specific resources.

SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC08.name: Multi-tenant or shared clusters
SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC08.desc: Managed services (cloud-hosted Redis, Memcached) provisioned with default credentials shared across multiple environments/customers due to misconfiguration.

SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC09.name: Database bootstrapping with seed data includes defaults
SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC09.desc: Initial setup scripts or configuration management (Ansible, Chef, Puppet) includes default creds in templates.

SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC10.name: Credential file permissions too open
SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC10.desc: Configuration files containing default credentials readable by all users on system (644 permissions instead of 600).

SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC11.name: Version upgrades preserve defaults
SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC11.desc: Database upgraded/restarted but credential configuration from before upgrade still applies; defaults re-enabled.

SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC12.name: Backup/recovery uses default creds
SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC12.desc: Restored databases or snapshots restore with original default credentials instead of new ones.

SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC13.name: Development credentials promoted to prod
SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC13.desc: Copy of development database snapshot with development default credentials used in production.

SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC14.name: Service account password never initialized
SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC14.desc: Aerospike, etcd, or other system service account created at install with no password; vulnerable to lateral movement.

SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC15.name: Third-party tools/integrations use defaults
SEC-KV-AUTH-003-RC15.desc: Monitoring agents, backup tools, or integration services connect using default credentials left unchanged.

SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC01.name: Memcached SASL authentication bypass (CVE-2016-8706)
SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC01.desc: Integer overflow in SASL auth processing allows attacker to craft malformed auth request bypassing validation; affects binary protocol only.

SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC02.name: Command injection in AUTH command
SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC02.desc: Specially crafted AUTH command or username with special characters bypasses parser; not sanitized before processing.

SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC03.name: Redis Lua script sandbox escape
SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC03.desc: CVE-2025-49844 (RediShell): authenticated attacker can escape Lua sandbox via use-after-free, but requires pre-authentication; however, can abuse with default/weak credentials.

SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC04.name: Aerospike privilege bypass via malformed selectors
SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC04.desc: Malformed ACL selectors trigger stack buffer overflow or logic bypass; authenticated user with limited privileges escalates.

SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC05.name: etcd RBAC logic bypass
SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC05.desc: Specially crafted etcd requests bypass RBAC checks; role/user validation not performed on certain command types or edge cases.

SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC06.name: DynamoDB IAM policy bypass
SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC06.desc: Overly permissive wildcards in IAM policy (`"Action": "dynamodb:*"`, `"Resource": "*"`) allow any authenticated principal to access all tables regardless of intended scope.

SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC07.name: Protected-mode can be disabled remotely (Redis)
SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC07.desc: If `CONFIG` command is not restricted via ACL, attacker disables `protected-mode` after gaining partial access: `CONFIG SET protected-mode no`.

SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC08.name: Authentication cached but not refreshed
SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC08.desc: Aerospike privilege-refresh-period (default 300s) allows stale permission use; permission revoked but attacker connection still active with old permissions.

SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC09.name: Null password handling
SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC09.desc: Parser treats empty string or null differently than expected; special cases in code allow bypass (e.g., Auth `""` interpreted as authenticated).

SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC10.name: Buffer overflow in auth parsing
SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC10.desc: Fixed-size buffer for username/password allows overflow; attacker writes shellcode or ROP gadgets to escape auth check.

SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC11.name: Race condition in auth state machine
SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC11.desc: Multi-threaded auth processing has TOCTOU (time-of-check-time-of-use) flaw; connection marked authenticated before final checks complete.

SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC12.name: Memcached UDP protocol reflection amplification
SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC12.desc: UDP-based protocol has no authentication; queries from any source processed and amplified, enabling DDoS and potential command execution.

SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC13.name: Protocol parsing ambiguity
SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC13.desc: Protocol specification ambiguous; client and server disagree on message boundaries allowing attacker to inject commands mid-stream.

SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC14.name: TLS certificate validation bypass
SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC14.desc: etcd client certificate auth not validated properly; self-signed cert or wrong CN accepted; certificate parsing logic flawed.

SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC15.name: Reverse engineering AUTH mechanism
SEC-KV-AUTH-004-RC15.desc: Custom authentication protocol reverse-engineered; attacker crafts valid auth responses without knowing password.

SEC-KV-AUTHZ-001-RC01.desc: Default “open” configuration left unchanged after installation, with built‑in users or roles retaining full access.
