SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC02.desc: Administrators are unaware of safer alternatives such as restricted export directories, parameterized export functions, or file-based I/O limitations; they grant full FILE privilege instead.

SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC03.name: Business intelligence and reporting tool requirements
SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC03.desc: BI tools and reporting applications request FILE access to write query results to files; rather than implementing tools with built-in safe export mechanisms, FILE privilege is granted.

SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC06.name: Developer convenience during development
SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC06.desc: File privileges are granted to development accounts for testing; these elevated permissions are then copied to production accounts without being removed.

SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC07.name: Troubleshooting and ad-hoc data extraction
SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC07.desc: DBAs grant FILE privilege for temporary troubleshooting (dumping data to files for analysis) or ad-hoc data extraction requests; the privilege is not revoked after the task completes.

SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC03.name: Convenience for distributed access management
SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC03.desc: Rather than centralizing permission administration, administrators grant WITH GRANT OPTION to department leads or team managers to distribute permissions; this delegates security control without oversight.

SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC08.name: Third-party tool or vendor requirements
SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC08.desc: ETL tools, backup solutions, or vendor applications explicitly require FILE or COPY privileges; organizations grant these without evaluating whether safer alternatives exist.

SEC-SQL-ENC-005-RC02.name: Short Key Lengths Selected for Performance
SEC-SQL-ENC-005-RC02.desc: Organizations configured encryption algorithms with short key lengths (128-bit instead of 256-bit AES, 1024-bit RSA instead of 2048-bit) to minimize CPU overhead.

SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC09.name: Historical privilege accumulation
SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC09.desc: File privileges were granted years ago for purposes that no longer apply; they are never audited or revoked.

SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC10.name: Insufficient monitoring of FILE privilege usage
SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC10.desc: No auditing or monitoring occurs to track which users exercise FILE privilege, for what purposes, or with what frequency; privilege grants cannot be justified or revoked.

SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC11.name: Shared service accounts with FILE privilege
SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC11.desc: Batch job and application service accounts share FILE privilege; removing the privilege would require refactoring multiple systems.

SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC12.name: Configuration management errors
SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC12.desc: Database provisioning scripts or configuration templates incorrectly grant FILE privilege to broader user sets than intended.

SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC01.name: Overly broad delegation of grant rights
SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC01.desc: Administrators grant users the WITH GRANT OPTION to allow them to delegate permissions, without clear restrictions on what permissions can be delegated or to whom.

SEC-SQL-AUD-014-RC04.name: Database link or synonym to external system created
SEC-SQL-AUD-014-RC04.desc: A CREATE DATABASE LINK, CREATE SYNONYM, sp_addlinkedserver, or CREATE FOREIGN DATA WRAPPER command establishes a connection pathway to an external database, which could be used to exfiltrate data or pivot to another system.

SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC05.name: Inadequate monitoring of grant activity
SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC05.desc: No logging or alerting occurs when users exercise WITH GRANT OPTION to grant permissions to others; privilege escalation chains are never detected.

SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC06.name: Lack of restrictions on re-delegation
SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC06.desc: Users with WITH GRANT OPTION can grant permissions to others, who can then grant those permissions further; uncontrolled privilege cascading occurs.

SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC07.name: Grant option on sensitive privileges
SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC07.desc: WITH GRANT OPTION is granted on high-risk privileges (e.g., SUPERUSER, ALTER SYSTEM, CREATE ROLE) that should never be delegated.

SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC08.name: Default role configurations including grant option
SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC08.desc: Predefined roles created during database setup include WITH GRANT OPTION without documented justification; administrators inherit these settings without review.

SEC-SQL-AUD-014-RC05.name: Account unlocked or expiry removed on dormant account
SEC-SQL-AUD-014-RC05.desc: An ALTER USER ... ACCOUNT UNLOCK, ENABLE LOGIN, or password-expiry-removal command reactivates a previously locked or expired account, which may be an attacker restoring access to a previously compromised credential.

SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC11.name: Application Middleware Bypass
SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC11.desc: Applications connect directly to the database, bypassing middleware and service meshes that could enforce encryption, because they were not designed with this architecture.

SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC09.name: Privilege escalation through role membership
SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC09.desc: Users granted WITH GRANT OPTION on a role can grant that role to themselves or others, effectively escalating their own privileges.

SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC10.name: Separation of duties violations
SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC10.desc: A single user with both elevated privileges AND WITH GRANT OPTION can grant those same privileges to other users, creating uncontrolled privilege proliferation.

SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC12.name: Testing and Development Environment Carryover
SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC12.desc: Unencrypted connections configured for testing environments are carried over to production without modification.

SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC13.name: Inherited permissions from legacy systems
SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC13.desc: Users have WITH GRANT OPTION from configurations created years ago; no one questions whether the original justification still applies.

SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC05.name: Database Mail and Service Broker Legacy Code
SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC05.desc: SQL Server Database Mail requires TLS 1.0 in some configurations (as of search results), forcing organizations to keep TLS 1.0 enabled at the OS level for the entire database to function.

SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC03.name: Backward Compatibility Requirements
SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC03.desc: Legacy applications were built against database clients that lack TLS 1.2+ support. Enabling encryption would break these applications, forcing a choice between security and functionality.

SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC04.name: Client Driver Version Mismatch
SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC04.desc: Older versions of database drivers (ODBC, JDBC, client libraries) do not support encryption or only support deprecated protocols. Applications cannot upgrade drivers without extensive testing and potential code changes.

SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC07.name: Certificate Management Complexity
SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC07.desc: Organizations have not established processes for generating, storing, distributing, and renewing SSL/TLS certificates across all database clients and servers. This operational complexity deters implementation.

SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC08.name: Self-Signed Certificate Issues
SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC08.desc: Certificate validation failures occur when using self-signed certificates without proper trust chains. Organizations disable certificate verification (`trustServerCertificate=true`) rather than resolving root CA trust problems.

SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC02.name: Missing Encryption Parameter in Connection Strings
SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC02.desc: Applications and client tools use connection strings without the vendor-specific encryption parameter, resulting in unencrypted connections by default.

SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC13.name: Inadequate Monitoring and Visibility
SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC13.desc: Organizations lack tools to detect or audit whether connections are encrypted, making unencrypted connections invisible until a security audit reveals them.

SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC01.name: Legacy Application Dependency on TLS 1.0/1.1
SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC01.desc: Older applications and client libraries explicitly require TLS 1.0 or 1.1 due to age (pre-2010 development). Disabling these protocols breaks application functionality.

SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC04.name: Key Management System Not Available
SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC04.desc: Organizations lack an external key management system (HSM, AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault) or knowledge of how to set one up. TDE requires a secure key store.

SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC02.name: Licensing Restrictions
SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC02.desc: TDE requires premium edition licensing or add-on options. Organizations use standard editions or lack budget for the required license upgrades.

SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC06.name: Database Design Incompatibility
SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC06.desc: Existing databases have design issues (unsupported data types, indexing constraints, compatibility with encrypted columns) that prevent TDE implementation without major refactoring.

SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC11.name: High Availability and Replication Issues
SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC11.desc: TDE adds complexity to failover, replication, and cluster configurations. Organizations avoid TDE to simplify high-availability operations.

SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC03.name: Key Management for Backups Not Established
SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC03.desc: Even if encryption is configured, the organization has not established secure key management for backup decryption. Backup encryption keys are stored alongside backup files or not backed up, making recovery impossible.

SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC05.name: Performance Impact on Backup Windows
SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC05.desc: Encrypting backups adds CPU overhead and I/O load, extending backup windows beyond acceptable limits. The organization chose speed over security.

SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC11.name: Database Encryption Complexity Misunderstood
SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC11.desc: Organizations with Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) enabled mistakenly believe backups are automatically encrypted because TDE encrypts the database. They do not realize that backup encryption requires separate configuration.

SEC-SQL-ENC-005-RC01.name: Default/Legacy Cipher Suites Not Disabled
SEC-SQL-ENC-005-RC01.desc: Database configurations enable weak cipher suites (RC4, DES, 3DES, MD5-signed certificates, CBC mode) for backward compatibility. Organizations have not explicitly disabled these weaker algorithms.

SEC-SQL-ENC-005-RC14.name: No Monitoring of Negotiated Ciphers
SEC-SQL-ENC-005-RC14.desc: The organization does not monitor or audit which cipher suites are actually being negotiated in real TLS connections. Weak ciphers might be in use even if stronger ones are configured.

SEC-SQL-ENC-005-RC16.name: Vendor Default Cipher Suites Used Without Review
SEC-SQL-ENC-005-RC16.desc: The organization trusts vendor defaults for cipher suite selection and has not evaluated whether these defaults meet security standards.

SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC03.name: Audit policy set to "NONE"
SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC03.desc: The audit policy is defined but explicitly configured to capture nothing (e.g., an empty rule set or a "disable" flag within the policy itself).

SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC05.name: Service account permission failures
SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC05.desc: The database service account lacks write permissions to the designated log directory, causing the logging subsystem to fail silently or disable itself.

SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC06.name: Performance-based disablement
SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC06.desc: Administrators intentionally disabled logging during a high-load event to reduce I/O or CPU overhead and failed to re-enable it.

SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC07.name: Misconfigured log destination
SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC07.desc: Logging is enabled, but the destination is set to a non-existent path, `/dev/null`, or a remote syslog server that is unreachable, effectively dropping all logs.

SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC03.name: Peer authentication misunderstood as secure
SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC03.desc: DBAs confuse `peer` (secure for local Unix sockets) with `trust` (unconditional) and leave `trust` enabled for TCP/IP thinking it's equivalent.

SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC05.name: Performance Impact Concerns
SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC05.desc: Organizations measured or heard about TDE performance overhead (8-12% for TDE, typically 5-6% per encrypted column) and concluded the cost was not justified.

SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC08.name: Default "Secure by Default" settings
SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC08.desc: The database was installed with factory defaults, which often favor performance over observability, leaving auditing disabled until explicitly turned on.

SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC09.name: Conflicting configuration files
SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC09.desc: A secondary configuration file (e.g., `conf.d/override.cnf`) is loading after the main config and overwriting the "enabled" setting with "disabled."

SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC10.name: Plugin initialization failure
SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC10.desc: The audit plugin failed to initialize during startup (due to memory constraints or dependency errors), forcing the database to start without auditing.

SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC11.name: Container/Ephemeral storage misconfiguration
SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC11.desc: In containerized environments, logs are written to an ephemeral path that is destroyed on restart, creating the appearance of disabled logging.

SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC01.name: Aggressive rotation configuration
SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC01.desc: Log rotation settings (time-based or size-based) are too aggressive, overwriting files faster than the compliance window (e.g., rotating every hour with only 10 files kept).

SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC02.name: Insufficient disk space
SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC02.desc: The partition dedicated to logs is too small, forcing automated cleanup scripts or the database itself to delete older logs to prevent server downtime.

SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC03.name: Lack of external archival
SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC03.desc: Logs are stored locally on the database server without a process (like `logrotate` or Splunk forwarders) to ship them to long-term storage (S3, cold storage) before deletion.

SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC14.name: Active transactions reading/writing sensitive columns (PII)
SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC14.desc: Currently-running queries reference tables that contain columns with sensitive names (password, ssn, credit card, email, etc.). Each row links a live transaction to a specific sensitive column it touches, including the executing login, host, program, and full SQL text. This is real-time PII exposure evidence — useful for compliance audits, DAM (Database Activity Monitoring), and forensic investigation of who accesses sensitive data.

SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC04.name: Default retention policies
SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC04.desc: The database is using default retention settings (often 7-30 days) which do not meet the 90+ day compliance requirement.

SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC06.name: Misconfigured "Purge" jobs
SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC06.desc: Automated scheduled tasks (cron jobs or internal DB schedulers) are configured with the wrong retention calculation (e.g., `DELETE < GETDATE() - 7` instead of `90`).

SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC07.name: File system quotas
SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC07.desc: The operating system user running the database has hit a file count or size quota, preventing new logs from being written or forcing immediate deletion of old ones.

SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC07.name: Application Testing Not Completed
SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC07.desc: TDE was evaluated but applications were not thoroughly tested with encrypted databases. Failures in testing (incompatible queries, timeouts) caused implementation to be abandoned.

SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC10.name: Manual deletion by admins
SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC10.desc: Administrators manually clear log files to free up space during disk pressure incidents, creating gaps in the audit trail.

SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC12.name: Sensitive columns discovered in schema (PII)
SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC12.desc: Database schema contains columns with names that strongly suggest PII or sensitive data (SSN, credit card, password, email, salary, etc.) that may not be encrypted, masked, or otherwise protected. These columns represent a compliance risk under GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS, and similar regulations.

SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC01.name: Insecure file permissions
SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC01.desc: The operating system directory storing audit logs has `777` (world-writable) permissions, allowing any user to delete or modify log files.

SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC02.name: Internal audit tables are mutable
SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC02.desc: Audit logs are stored in standard database tables that can be updated or truncated by users with `DBA` or `SUPERUSER` privileges.

SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC03.name: Lack of File Integrity Monitoring (FIM)
SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC03.desc: No external security tool (like OSSEC or Tripwire) is monitoring the log files, so tampering goes undetected.

SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC04.name: Service account ownership
SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC04.desc: The database service account owns the log files and the database process itself can be manipulated (e.g., via SQL injection or stored procedure) to overwrite them.

SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC05.name: Missing "Append-Only" attributes
SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC05.desc: The filesystem does not use "append-only" attributes (`chattr +a` on Linux), allowing files to be truncated or deleted.

SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC06.name: Audit logs not shipped remotely
SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC06.desc: Logs exist *only* on the database server. If an attacker gains root/admin access, they can wipe the only copy of the evidence.

SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC08.name: Admin accounts shared/untracked
SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC08.desc: Multiple users share a generic "admin" login, making it impossible to attribute the deletion of logs to a specific individual.

SEC-SQL-AUD-004-RC04.name: Generic "Audit All" disabled
SEC-SQL-AUD-004-RC04.desc: The global audit switch is on, but the specific subclass for "Session/Connection" events is disabled.

SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC09.name: Audit disablement capability
SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC09.desc: High-privileged users have the permission to turn off the auditing system temporarily, perform actions, and turn it back on without a trace of the disablement itself (if that event isn't logged elsewhere).

SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC04.name: Logging "Write" vs "DDL"
SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC04.desc: The configuration enables "Write" auditing (data modification) but treats "DDL" (schema modification) as a separate category that was left disabled.

SEC-SQL-AUD-004-RC02.name: "Successful Logins Only" filter
SEC-SQL-AUD-004-RC02.desc: The audit policy is explicitly configured to log only *successful* connections to reduce noise, blinding the system to brute force attacks.

SEC-SQL-AUD-004-RC03.name: Connection string errors
SEC-SQL-AUD-004-RC03.desc: Connection attempts that fail at the network/listener level (before reaching the database engine) are not logged by the DB, only by the firewall or OS.

SEC-SQL-AUD-004-RC07.name: Internal vs External Authentication
SEC-SQL-AUD-004-RC07.desc: The database relies on external auth (LDAP/Kerberos). Failures happen at the Identity Provider level and are never sent to the database to be logged.

SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC13.name: Sensitive columns actively queried (PII in use)
SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC13.desc: Columns identified as containing PII or sensitive data are actively being accessed by queries. This indicates live exposure risk — sensitive data is not just stored but actively read, potentially by applications, reports, or ad-hoc queries without proper masking or access controls.

SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC01.name: DML-focused Audit Policy
SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC01.desc: The audit configuration focuses solely on data access (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`), ignoring schema changes (`CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`).

SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC02.name: Granularity settings
SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC02.desc: The logging level is set to "Statement" or "Query" but includes a filter that excludes specific keywords like `ALTER` or `DROP`.

SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC03.name: Privileged User Exclusion
SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC03.desc: DDL is often performed by Superusers/DBAs, but the audit policy explicitly excludes the "admin" user to reduce log volume.

SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC05.name: Deployment via Scripts
SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC05.desc: DDL changes are applied via automated deployment scripts using a specific service account that is whitelisted/excluded from auditing.

SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC07.name: Extension/Plugin Limitations
SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC07.desc: The installed auditing plugin only supports capturing DML events and lacks the hooks to intercept DDL commands.

SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC08.name: Statement Truncation
SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC08.desc: DDL statements are logged, but the log buffer size is too small, truncating the query string so the actual `ALTER` command is unreadable.

SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC01.name: Bind Address Misconfiguration
SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC01.desc: Database configured to listen on 0.0.0.0 or all IPv4/IPv6 addresses instead of localhost (127.0.0.1) or specific private IPs. Default configurations in some setup guides recommend this for development convenience without emphasizing production security implications.

SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC02.name: Overly Permissive Security Group/Firewall Rules
SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC02.desc: Network access controls configured to allow inbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 (any IP) on database ports. Often created as temporary measures during troubleshooting that become permanent.

SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC04.name: Documentation Focuses on Default Values
SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC04.desc: Deployment guides, tutorials, and quick-start documentation use default ports. Administrators follow these without considering security implications.

SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC05.name: Lack of IP Allowlist/Whitelist Enforcement
SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC05.desc: No explicit controls restricting database access to known, specific IP addresses or CIDR blocks of legitimate clients.

SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC11.name: Shadow IT / Unauthorized Deployments
SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC11.desc: Database instances spun up by developers outside official deployment processes, bypassing security review and governance.

SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC12.name: Temporary Access Left Permanently
SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC12.desc: Security groups or firewall rules opened temporarily for debugging, testing, or rapid development never reverted to restrictive state.

SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC02.name: Lack of Security Hardening Process
SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC02.desc: No post-installation security hardening checklist. Default ports considered "good enough" if protected by other means (which often aren't).

SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC03.name: Convenience and Standardization
SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC03.desc: Teams use default ports to reduce configuration complexity and ensure consistency across environments. Non-default ports require additional documentation and coordination.

SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC12.name: Version Disclosure via Banners
SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC12.desc: Default ports combined with service banners reveal specific database software and versions, enabling version-specific exploitation.

SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC08.name: No Port Randomization or Obscurity Strategy
SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC08.desc: Organizations don't implement port randomization or assign non-standard ports. Treat port numbers as non-security-critical configuration.

SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC13.name: Brute Force Attack Simplification
SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC13.desc: Default ports reduce attacker reconnaissance time, enabling rapid brute force authentication attempts against commonly accessible database services.

SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC14.name: Lack of Port Rotation Practices
SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC14.desc: No periodic updates or changes to ports even when databases are patched or moved. Static port assignments become predictable targets.

SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC15.name: Automated Scanning Vulnerability
SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC15.desc: Internet-wide automated scanners probe default ports first. A significant portion of database breaches start with scanners finding services on default ports.

SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC11.name: Deprecated Flag Persistence
SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC11.desc: Older trace flags relevant to previous SQL Server versions (pre-2016) remain enabled even after upgrade to newer version where they're unnecessary

SEC-SQL-AUD-006-RC01.name: Privileged account executing DML outside maintenance window
SEC-SQL-AUD-006-RC01.desc: A superuser or DBA account runs INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE during normal business hours or outside a scheduled window, signalling unplanned or unauthorized data modification.

SEC-SQL-AUD-006-RC02.name: Superuser running ad-hoc queries on sensitive tables
SEC-SQL-AUD-006-RC02.desc: An admin account directly queries PII, credential, financial, or encryption-key tables outside an approved application context, indicating reconnaissance or exfiltration preparation.

SEC-SQL-AUD-006-RC03.name: High privilege account accessing schema outside designated scope
SEC-SQL-AUD-006-RC03.desc: An administrative account that normally operates within a specific schema begins accessing schemas or databases outside its designated boundary, suggesting lateral movement.

SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC03.name: Database Features Requiring Internet Access
SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC03.desc: Features like automatic updates, telemetry, cloud backups, external data wrapper connections, or plugin repositories require outbound internet connectivity. Enabled by default without evaluating necessity.

SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC05.name: External Data Source Integration
SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC05.desc: Databases configured to access external APIs, REST services, or data sources via UDFs (User Defined Functions) or stored procedures. No network policy restricting which external hosts can be reached.

SEC-SQL-CFG-001-RC03.name: Administrative Troubleshooting Convenience
SEC-SQL-CFG-001-RC03.desc: DBAs enable OS command execution for ad-hoc system administration tasks (file operations, command execution) rather than using proper automation tools or secure alternatives.

SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC14.name: Database Replication to Cloud
SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC14.desc: Hybrid environments requiring outbound connections for replication to cloud databases. Implemented without restricting destination endpoints.

SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC10.name: Insufficient RBAC Controls
SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC10.desc: Sample databases left with default permissions; no restriction preventing users from connecting to or querying test databases

SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC04.name: External data access configuration
SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC04.desc: Database features for querying external data sources (foreign data wrappers, linked servers, database links) establish arbitrary outbound connections. Configuration does not restrict allowed destination servers.

SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC13.name: Weak Object Naming Conventions
SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC13.desc: Sample databases not named distinctly enough to be easily identified (e.g., "test" is ambiguous); gets confused with legitimate test systems

SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC15.name: Monitoring and Logging Exfiltration
SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC15.desc: Databases with unrestricted access to send logs, metrics, and telemetry to external monitoring services. No whitelisting of logging destination IPs.

SEC-SQL-CFG-001-RC01.name: Legacy Application Compatibility
SEC-SQL-CFG-001-RC01.desc: Older applications written for SQL Server 2000/2005 era rely on xp_cmdshell for OS-level operations; migration to newer secure methods is deferred due to development resource constraints

SEC-SQL-CFG-001-RC06.name: Excessive Service Account Privileges
SEC-SQL-CFG-001-RC06.desc: SQL Server service account runs with Local System or administrator-level permissions; when xp_cmdshell is enabled, any command inherits these elevated privileges

SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC01.name: Default Installation Artifacts
SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC01.desc: Vendor installation scripts create sample databases (pubs, northwind, test) by default; scripts are run without review of what's being created

SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC02.name: Development Environment Cloning
SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC02.desc: Production database environments copied from development/test environments; sample schemas from dev environment remain present

SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC03.name: Backup Restoration Error
SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC03.desc: Backups taken from systems with sample databases are restored to production without pre-restore pruning of unnecessary objects

SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC07.name: Application Configuration Pointing to Wrong Database
SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC07.desc: Applications misconfigured to point at test/sample database instead of production database; remaining sample database "in case" needed

SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC08.name: Demonstration and Training Use
SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC08.desc: Sample databases left in place for new DBA training or vendor demonstrations; forgotten after training is complete

SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC14.name: Multi-Tenant Instance Management
SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC14.desc: On shared database instances, sample databases from one customer/application remain even as others are removed

SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC02.name: Performance Optimization
SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC02.desc: Legacy code paths use CLR for complex algorithmic operations rather than T-SQL; disabling CLR would require extensive refactoring

SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC13.name: Lack of Audit Trail
SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC13.desc: No mechanism to track when/why trace flags were enabled; difficult to justify continued use or identify candidates for removal

SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC04.name: Perceived Performance Optimization
SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC04.desc: DBA reads that a trace flag or parameter improves temporary tablespace or checkpoint behavior; enables it without baseline testing or comparative metrics

SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC02.name: Vendor/Support Recommendation
SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC02.desc: Vendor support or consulting recommends specific trace flag for compatibility or workaround; enabled without documented plan to remove

SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC06.name: Experimentation in Production
SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC06.desc: DBA testing different trace flag values directly in production to find optimal setting; tests never cleaned up

SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC07.name: One-Off Debugging Enabled Persistently
SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC07.desc: Trace flag enabled to diagnose specific deadlock or query issue; becomes permanent when logs stored for historical reference

SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC08.name: Configuration Drift
SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC08.desc: Trace flags configured in one environment (dev/test) and propagated to production via infrastructure-as-code without security review

SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC10.name: Verbose Logging for "Security"
SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC10.desc: Trace flags enabling query/transaction logging enabled as "security measure" but left on 24/7 causing performance and disk space issues

SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC12.name: Lazy Optimization
SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC12.desc: DBAs use trace flags as shortcut instead of properly tuning queries, indexes, or parameters; technical debt accumulates

SEC-SQL-AUD-006-RC04.name: Service account performing interactive or manual transactions
SEC-SQL-AUD-006-RC04.desc: A service or application account (expected to run only parameterized queries) is observed in an interactive session running ad-hoc SQL, indicating possible credential theft.

SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC01.name: String concatenation for query building
SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC01.desc: Developers directly concatenate user input or variables into SQL strings using language string operators without parameterization, treating the resulting string as executable code.

SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC02.name: Inadequate input validation and sanitization
SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC02.desc: Reliance on flawed or incomplete input validation, character escaping, or regex patterns that don't cover all injection vectors or can be bypassed by sophisticated attacks.

SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC04.name: Legacy code and technical debt
SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC04.desc: Older stored procedures were written before parameterized query awareness; refactoring is postponed due to cost, time constraints, and fears of breaking dependent applications.

SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC07.name: Mixing static and dynamic SQL constructs
SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC07.desc: Developers build WHERE clauses or query fragments dynamically, then pass them to prepared statements, creating a false sense of security when the structure itself can be altered by attackers.

SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC06.name: Crash Dumps and Core Files
SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC06.desc: When a database process crashes (e.g., Segfault), it writes a memory dump (core file) to disk. These dumps contain fragments of RAM which often hold clear text PII and passwords from recent queries.

SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC08.name: Complex business requirements
SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC08.desc: Multi-tenant systems, dynamic filtering, variable column selection, or reporting queries that require runtime table/column names appear impossible to implement with static SQL, leading developers to use dynamic SQL.

SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC09.name: Performance optimization assumptions
SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC09.desc: Misunderstanding that dynamic SQL might improve performance in certain scenarios; using EXEC with concatenated strings to avoid perceived query plan caching issues (actually inferior to parameterized queries).

SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC14.name: Implicit trust in framework defaults
SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC14.desc: Developers assume that using stored procedures inherently prevents SQL injection without realizing that dynamic SQL within stored procedures remains vulnerable.

SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC15.name: Incomplete parameter binding
SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC15.desc: Only some parameters are parameterized while others are concatenated; identifiers (table/column names) are concatenated because they cannot be parameterized, creating partial vulnerability. **Developer/Code Root Causes:** - **Rapid prototyping mentality** - Build functionality quickly first, refactor later; dynamic SQL is faster to write initially but riskier long-term. - **Knowledge gaps in secure patterns** - Developers trained on how to use stored procedures but not how to implement them securely with dynamic SQL. - **Misaligned incentives** - Success metrics focus on features delivered,...

SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC06.name: Operational automation dependencies
SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC06.desc: Database maintenance tasks (backup management, file system checks, log rotation, folder permissions) appear to require direct OS command execution from within the database.

SEC-SQL-AUD-006-RC05.name: Privilege escalation during active session
SEC-SQL-AUD-006-RC05.desc: A session that started with standard privileges subsequently executes GRANT, SET ROLE, or other privilege-elevating commands within the same connection.

SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC07.name: Insufficient privilege controls
SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC07.desc: Developers grant administrative roles too broadly or fail to restrict who can enable/execute OS commands; the feature becomes accessible to accounts that should not have it.

SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC12.name: Third-party application requirements
SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC12.desc: Vendor software or legacy applications explicitly require OS command execution; replacing or upgrading these systems is not feasible in the short term.

SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC13.name: Operator control issues
SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC13.desc: Database operators or administrators use OS command execution features in maintenance jobs because built-in administrative tasks do not fully meet operational requirements.

SEC-SQL-AUD-007-RC01.name: Transactions from unregistered application signatures
SEC-SQL-AUD-007-RC01.desc: SQL traffic originates from an application_name, client program, or connection tag not present in the approved application registry, suggesting a rogue or shadow tool.

SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC01.name: Legacy system constraints
SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC01.desc: Extended stored procedures (xp_* functions) were the primary mechanism for OS-level operations in older SQL Server versions; replacing them requires significant refactoring of existing applications.

SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC02.name: Deferred major version upgrades due to technical complexity
SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC02.desc: Major version upgrades require significant testing, potential data migration, application recompilation, or schema changes that demand substantial engineering effort, leading teams to postpone indefinitely.

SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC05.name: Application dependency on deprecated database features
SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC05.desc: Older applications may rely on deprecated database functions, syntax, or behavior no longer present in newer versions, requiring significant application refactoring or rewriting before migration is feasible.

SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC16.name: Insufficient removal validation
SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC16.desc: When OS command execution is removed, hidden dependencies may exist in scheduled jobs, maintenance plans, or third-party tools; removal causes unexpected failures in production.

SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC09.name: Client and driver compatibility concerns
SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC09.desc: Applications using database clients or drivers compiled against older versions may require relinking, recompilation, or updates that demand coordination across multiple teams and application owners.

SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC11.name: Legacy application portfolio constraints
SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC11.desc: Some business-critical legacy applications were built on specific database versions and have not been maintained; attempting upgrades risks breaking these unsupported, unmaintained systems.

SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC12.name: Incremental neglect over multiple release cycles
SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC12.desc: Organizations miss several consecutive EOL deadlines (e.g., "we'll upgrade from 11 to 12 eventually"), allowing the problem to compound until the cost becomes prohibitive.

SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC05.name: Sensitive Functions in Logs
SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC05.desc: Even with some masking, specific functions like `PASSWORD()`, `AES_ENCRYPT('data', 'secret_key')`, or `MD5()` often bypass log redaction filters because the database logger sees them as standard function calls, logging the literal 'secret_key'.

SEC-SQL-AUD-007-RC02.name: Query patterns not matching known application baseline
SEC-SQL-AUD-007-RC02.desc: Queries exhibit structural signatures (table combinations, column access, JOIN depth) that do not appear in the established workload fingerprint, indicating manually crafted or injected SQL.

SEC-SQL-AUD-007-RC03.name: Connections from unexpected network addresses
SEC-SQL-AUD-007-RC03.desc: Active database sessions originate from IP ranges or hostnames not listed in the approved connection whitelist, indicating an unauthorized client.

SEC-SQL-AUD-007-RC04.name: Off-hours transaction activity from non-automated accounts
SEC-SQL-AUD-007-RC04.desc: Human-owned accounts generate database activity during nights, weekends, or holidays when no scheduled batch jobs are expected, consistent with unauthorized access.

SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC15.name: SQL injection chaining
SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC15.desc: If any application connected to SQL Server is vulnerable to SQL injection, attackers can exploit it to execute arbitrary xp_cmdshell commands without direct database access.

SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC04.name: Audit Trail Over-Configuration
SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC04.desc: Audit policies configured to capture full SQL text or bind variable values to meet compliance, unintentionally recording sensitive inputs in the audit trail.

SEC-SQL-PAT-002-RC02.name: Extended CVE disclosure-to-patch timelines
SEC-SQL-PAT-002-RC02.desc: Vulnerabilities often remain unpatched for 30-90+ days between rootcause disclosure and organizational patch deployment, during which active exploitation occurs.

SEC-SQL-PAT-002-RC09.name: Incompatible dependency chains
SEC-SQL-PAT-002-RC09.desc: Applying a database patch may require updating dependent libraries, frameworks, or client drivers that themselves have unpatched vulnerabilities, creating a dependency resolution nightmare.

SEC-SQL-PAT-002-RC10.name: Active database usage preventing maintenance windows
SEC-SQL-PAT-002-RC10.desc: Business demands for 24/7 availability eliminate maintenance windows needed for patch testing and deployment.

SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC07.name: Slow Query Logs with Low Thresholds
SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC07.desc: The "Slow Query Log" is enabled with a threshold of 0 seconds (or very low) to catch performance issues, effectively turning it into a general query log that captures data-heavy insert/update statements.

SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC01.name: Misunderstanding of "Encryption at Rest" (TDE)
SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC01.desc: Teams often enable Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) or disk-level encryption (e.g., AWS EBS encryption) and believe the data is secure. This protects physical drives but *automatically decrypts* data for any valid user or application connection, leaving PII exposed to SQL injection or rogue DBAs.

SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC09.name: Key Management Complexity
SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC09.desc: The team lacks a secure Key Management Service (KMS). Because they don't know where to safely store the encryption keys, they hardcode them or avoid encryption entirely to prevent "losing the data" if keys are lost.

SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC02.name: Searchability \& Indexing Requirements
SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC02.desc: Applications often need to search, sort, or join on PII fields (e.g., "Find user by email"). Encrypting these columns (using randomized encryption) breaks indexing and search capability, so developers default to clear text to maintain performance.

SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC04.name: Incorrect Data Types
SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC04.desc: Schema designers use standard `TEXT`, `VARCHAR`, or `CHAR` types for PII instead of `VARBINARY` or `BYTEA`. This forces the data to be stored as readable strings rather than the binary output of an encryption function.

SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC05.name: Legacy Schema Constraints
SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC05.desc: The database was designed years ago without encryption. Altering the schema now to change column types and update all application queries to handle encryption/decryption is viewed as too high-risk or expensive (Technical Debt).

SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC06.name: In-House "Masking" Logic Failure
SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC06.desc: Instead of true encryption, developers apply simple obfuscation (e.g., Base64 encoding or custom bit-shifting) which looks secure but is trivially reversible (clear text equivalent).

SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC11.name: Unsecured Backups/Snapshots
SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC11.desc: Database backups or snapshots are taken without encryption. Even if the live DB is secure, a developer restoring a production snapshot to a lower environment exposes the clear text PII.

SEC-SQL-AUD-008-RC04.name: Transactions accessing credential or encryption key tables
SEC-SQL-AUD-008-RC04.desc: Any account other than the designated key-management service queries tables that store hashed passwords, API keys, or encryption key material.

SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC02.name: Unparameterized Queries (String Concatenation)
SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC02.desc: Developers build SQL queries using string concatenation (e.g., `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE ssn = '" + ssn_var + "'"`). This sends the literal PII value to the database log. Parameterized queries (using `?` or `$1`) would only log the query structure, not the sensitive data.

SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC10.name: Lack of Native Masking Features (Old Versions)
SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC10.desc: Older database versions lacked native Dynamic Data Masking (DDM) features, leading to clear text storage as the default behavior unless custom views or application-level masking were built.

SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC11.name: Insufficient Log Rotation/Permissions
SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC11.desc: Logs containing sensitive data are written to world-readable directories (`/tmp` or `/var/log`) and are not rotated/deleted frequently enough, allowing long-term accumulation of sensitive history.

SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC09.name: Trace Files left Enabled
SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC09.desc: Database tracing or profiling tools enabled for debugging and left active after the session. These trace files capture query text and bind variable values containing sensitive data.

SEC-SQL-AU-002-RC02.name: SQL Server Windows Auth mode conversion
SEC-SQL-AU-002-RC02.desc: When changing SQL Server from Windows Authentication to Mixed Mode without proper setup, the sa account may retain an empty password from initial installation.

SEC-SQL-AU-001-RC02.name: Installation mode misalignment
SEC-SQL-AU-001-RC02.desc: Choosing a restricted authentication mode during installation disables the default superuser account, but later switching to a more permissive mode without explicitly setting a strong password leaves the account empty or unchanged.

SEC-SQL-AU-001-RC05.name: Knowledge gap on account purposes
SEC-SQL-AU-001-RC05.desc: DBAs don't understand which default accounts are system-critical versus removable sample or demo accounts, leading to inconsistent remediation of default credentials.

SEC-SQL-AU-004-RC04.name: OS-integrated authentication trust configuration
SEC-SQL-AU-004-RC04.desc: Database configured to trust OS-level or directory-service authentication for remote access, assuming that OS or domain security is equivalent to database security.

SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC07.name: Configuration file management tools
SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC07.desc: Ansible, Terraform, or other infrastructure-as-code templates use default database authentication configuration without customization; automated deployments inherit insecure defaults.

SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC01.name: Global "Log Everything" Configuration
SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC01.desc: Database query logging configured to capture all SQL statements, including those containing PII literals in INSERT, UPDATE, or WHERE clauses. Left enabled after debugging, it exposes sensitive data in plain text log files.

SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC12.name: Cloud Database Settings
SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC12.desc: In cloud environments (RDS, Azure SQL), TDE may be disabled by default, and organizations do not enable it because they assume the cloud provider's encryption is sufficient (confusion with AWS/Azure managed encryption at the storage level).

SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC04.name: Inadequate file operation path restrictions
SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC04.desc: Database file operation path restrictions are not properly configured to constrain file import/export to safe directories, granting uncontrolled filesystem access to accounts with file operation privileges.

SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC07.name: System database requirements
SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC07.desc: SQL Server system databases (master, msdb, tempdb) require cross-database chaining to be enabled; administrators may then inadvertently enable it at the server level for all databases.

SEC-SQL-AU-002-RC01.name: Initialization flag usage
SEC-SQL-AU-002-RC01.desc: Database initialization flag or mode creates the default superuser account with an empty password intentionally (for local testing convenience), but the insecure configuration remains in place when deployed to production.

SEC-SQL-AU-002-RC05.name: Password never set in configuration
SEC-SQL-AU-002-RC05.desc: Default superuser account does not require a password for OS-authenticated local connections, but when remote access is later enabled, no password has been set, leaving the account exposed.

SEC-SQL-AU-002-RC08.name: SQL Server's legacy behavior
SEC-SQL-AU-002-RC08.desc: Older SQL Server installations or misconfigurations where the sa account password is set to empty string, and administrators are unaware it's still empty.

SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC02.name: Complexity enforcement disabled intentionally
SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC02.desc: Password complexity enforcement policy disabled intentionally to ease administration or reduce user friction, without recognizing the security trade-off of allowing weak passwords.

SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC10.name: Container/Kubernetes secrets practice
SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC10.desc: In containerized database deployments, passwordless local authentication is enabled because the environment is assumed to be isolated, ignoring that other containers or pod sidecars on the same host can access the database.

SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC11.name: Single-node assumption
SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC11.desc: Developers assume the database is single-machine; passwordless local authentication seems safe until replication, clustering, or remote backup tools are added and expose the permissive configuration.

SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC14.name: No configuration drift detection
SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC14.desc: Database authentication configurations are not regularly scanned for unauthorized or overly permissive authentication entries.

SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC01.name: Application requirements for file export functionality
SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC01.desc: Applications legitimately need to export data to files; filesystem access privileges are granted to application service accounts to support this feature.

SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC14.name: DLL file vulnerabilities
SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC14.desc: Extended procedures are implemented as DLL files loaded into SQL Server memory; bugs in these DLLs can cause buffer overflows, crashes, or memory corruption exploitable for arbitrary code execution.

SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC03.name: Verbose Error Logging
SEC-SQL-PRI-002-RC03.desc: Error logging configured to include the SQL statement that caused the failure. When a PII-laden query fails, the full query text with sensitive data is written to the error log.

SEC-SQL-AUD-022-RC01.name: Unsuccessful database authentication attempts detected
SEC-SQL-AUD-022-RC01.desc: Detects failed (unsuccessful) database login attempts - e.g. an invalid password. Oracle: UNIFIED_AUDIT_TRAIL LOGON with return_code <> 0 (1017 = invalid credentials). SQL Server: xp_readerrorlog 'Login failed' from the ERRORLOG (default failed-login auditing). MySQL/MariaDB: performance_schema.host_cache.COUNT_AUTHENTICATION_ERRORS. Verify by attempting a login with an invalid password.

SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC10.name: Temporary workspace encryption complications
SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC10.desc: Organizations are aware that enabling TDE on a user database automatically encrypts the temporary tablespace, creating unexpected encryption scope and overhead, and chose not to enable TDE to avoid this.

SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC06.name: Development environment consistency
SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC06.desc: Development systems run in Mixed Mode (more flexible), and that configuration is replicated to production without review.

SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC04.name: License restrictions
SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC04.desc: Advanced auditing features (common in Enterprise editions) are installed but disabled because a valid license key was not detected, causing the plugin to shut down.

SEC-SQL-AUD-023-RC01.name: User account created (CREATE USER/LOGIN/ROLE)
SEC-SQL-AUD-023-RC01.desc: User account created (CREATE USER/LOGIN/ROLE). Part of DBA / administrator activity monitoring. Oracle reads UNIFIED_AUDIT_TRAIL; SQL Server reads the plan cache (dm_exec_query_stats); MySQL/MariaDB read performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest. Verify by performing the action.

SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC08.name: Circular log overwrite
SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC08.desc: The auditing system is configured in a "circular" mode where it writes to a fixed-size file that overwrites itself once full, regardless of time elapsed.

SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC09.name: Container restart data loss
SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC09.desc: In Kubernetes/Docker, logs are written to the container's stdout/stderr without a sidecar or logging driver to capture and persist them past the container's lifecycle.

SEC-SQL-AUD-023-RC02.name: Privileges granted (possible excessive grant)
SEC-SQL-AUD-023-RC02.desc: Privileges granted (possible excessive grant). Part of DBA / administrator activity monitoring. Oracle reads UNIFIED_AUDIT_TRAIL; SQL Server reads the plan cache (dm_exec_query_stats); MySQL/MariaDB read performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest. Verify by performing the action.

SEC-SQL-AUD-023-RC03.name: User account dropped (DROP USER/LOGIN/ROLE)
SEC-SQL-AUD-023-RC03.desc: User account dropped (DROP USER/LOGIN/ROLE). Part of DBA / administrator activity monitoring. Oracle reads UNIFIED_AUDIT_TRAIL; SQL Server reads the plan cache (dm_exec_query_stats); MySQL/MariaDB read performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest. Verify by performing the action.

SEC-SQL-AUD-024-RC01.name: SELECT access to designated sensitive tables detected
SEC-SQL-AUD-024-RC01.desc: Captures SELECT access to designated sensitive business-data tables (Flexcube customer/account PII: FSDH_CUSTOMER_BVN, STTM_Customer, STTM_Cust_Account, STTM_Personal, STTM_Corporate ...). Oracle reads V$SQL (command_type=3, plan cache); SQL Server reads dm_exec_query_stats; MySQL/MariaDB read performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest. The table list is embedded in the rule SQL - edit it to add/adjust sensitive objects. Verify by running a SELECT against a listed table.

SEC-SQL-QE-001-RC01.name: Stored procedure slower than its historical average
SEC-SQL-QE-001-RC01.desc: A user stored procedure is executing slower than that procedure's own historical average duration. System ('sys') procedures and system databases are excluded. Sustained or repeated regressions can indicate parameter sniffing, stale statistics, plan changes, blocking/resource contention, or anomalous/abusive use.

SEC-SQL-AUTHZ-001-RC01.name: Database access & privilege inventory (logins, roles, grants)
SEC-SQL-AUTHZ-001-RC01.desc: Enumerates, for every online user database on the instance, each database principal mapped to its server login, the database roles it belongs to, and its explicit permission grants - a Server -> Database -> Login -> roles & grants inventory for access review.

SEC-SQL-ACC-011-RC02.name: Active transactions (excluding monitoring user)
SEC-SQL-ACC-011-RC02.desc: All currently open / in-flight user transactions on the instance, excluding the dbdome monitoring login (dbd_mon_usr / dbdome_mon_usr). Surfaces who is holding a transaction, against which database, for how long, the transaction state and the SQL text - for spotting long-running or abandoned transactions, blocking, and anomalous activity.

SEC-SQL-DSC-001-RC01.name: Server data hierarchy (databases -> schemas -> tables -> columns)
SEC-SQL-DSC-001-RC01.desc: Enumerates the full data hierarchy of the server: every user database, its schemas, tables and columns (with data type). Powers the server/data tree used to select where RBAC and data-protection controls apply.

SEC-SQL-DSC-002-RC01.name: RBAC inventory (server roles, db roles, logins, users)
SEC-SQL-DSC-002-RC01.desc: Lists every server role, login, database role and database user on the server (tagged by principal_type), so the RBAC dashboard can show each in its own panel.

SEC-SQL-AU-001-RC04.name: Lack of post-deployment hardening checklist
SEC-SQL-AU-001-RC04.desc: Organizations deploy databases following application-focused checklists that omit security hardening steps, particularly default account remediation.

SEC-SQL-AU-001-RC06.name: Incomplete migration procedures
SEC-SQL-AU-001-RC06.desc: When moving from development to production, default accounts created in dev environments are not reviewed or removed during promotion.

SEC-SQL-AU-001-RC11.name: Inadequate change control
SEC-SQL-AU-001-RC11.desc: Post-installation account changes lack change order tracking, so when environments are rebuilt or cloned, original default credentials return without verification.

SEC-SQL-AU-002-RC06.name: Identity provisioning tool failure
SEC-SQL-AU-002-RC06.desc: IAM systems that create database accounts may fail on the final password-setting step while leaving the account created and enabled with empty password set flag.

SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC04.name: Regulatory compliance misinterpretation
SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC04.desc: NIST 800-63 recommendations (longer passphrases without complexity) are misinterpreted as no complexity required at all.

SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC05.name: Complexity vs. length tradeoff avoided
SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC05.desc: Organizations reject "complex" password policies thinking they'll switch to passphrase-based systems, but never implement the alternative.

SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC06.name: Performance concerns
SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC06.desc: Administrators believe password hashing/validation overhead is significant and weaken policies to reduce CPU cost, without evidence of actual impact.

SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC08.name: Development environment settings bleeding to production
SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC08.desc: Dev databases with relaxed policies are cloned or templated to production without policy review.

SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC10.name: Password manager unavailability
SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC10.desc: Absence of organizational password management tools leads administrators to assume users cannot handle complex passwords and weaken requirements.

SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC11.name: Lack of monitoring tools
SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC11.desc: Organizations without compromised credential monitoring don't perceive the risk of weak passwords and continue relaxed policies.

SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC12.name: Policy documentation missing
SEC-SQL-AU-003-RC12.desc: No written policy exists, so individual DBAs enforce their own (often minimal) standards.

SEC-SQL-AU-004-RC07.name: Cross-system domain trusts
SEC-SQL-AU-004-RC07.desc: Multiple database servers trust a single directory server (LDAP, AD) for authentication, but access controls aren't enforced per-database.

SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC01.name: Application compatibility requirement
SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC01.desc: Third-party or legacy applications don't support Windows Authentication, forcing Mixed Mode to support both SQL Auth and Windows Auth.

SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC02.name: Multi-tenancy needs
SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC02.desc: SaaS or multi-tenant deployments require SQL authentication for non-domain users, necessitating Mixed Mode alongside Windows Auth.

SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC03.name: Misguided "flexibility" goal
SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC03.desc: DBAs enable Mixed Mode thinking it provides optionality without understanding the attack surface expansion.

SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC04.name: Incomplete migration
SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC04.desc: Organizations migrating from SQL Auth to Windows Auth enable both temporarily "during transition" but never disable SQL Auth afterward.

SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC05.name: External contractor access
SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC05.desc: Contractors, vendors, or cloud-based applications need SQL authentication accounts because they're not in the Windows domain.

SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC07.name: Post-installation guidance misunderstood
SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC07.desc: Vendor installation documentation suggesting a permissive authentication mode for flexibility is followed without understanding the security implications.

SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC08.name: Service account password storage
SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC08.desc: Service accounts and scheduled jobs require stored SQL auth credentials, forcing Mixed Mode to be enabled for service account definition.

SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC09.name: No policy mandating Windows Auth
SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC09.desc: Organizations lack security policy requiring Windows Authentication only; Mixed Mode is permitted by default.

SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC10.name: Lateral movement not considered
SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC10.desc: Security teams don't recognize that Mixed Mode increases lateral movement risk if SQL credentials are compromised and used remotely.

SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC11.name: Kerberos delegation configuration complexity
SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC11.desc: Proper Windows Auth with delegation requires complex SPN and service account setup; Mixed Mode avoids this complexity.

SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC12.name: Application connection string defaults
SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC12.desc: ORM frameworks and libraries default to SQL authentication if not explicitly configured otherwise, encouraging Mixed Mode for simplicity.

SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC13.name: No automated compliance scanning
SEC-SQL-AU-005-RC13.desc: No tools check production databases and flag Mixed Mode as non-compliant.

SEC-SQL-AU-006-RC06.name: Test/dev accounts migrated to production
SEC-SQL-AU-006-RC06.desc: Development and testing accounts created in non-prod environments are cloned to production and left untouched.

SEC-SQL-AU-006-RC11.name: Account ownership unclear
SEC-SQL-AU-006-RC11.desc: Accounts lack documented owners; when owners leave or departments reorganize, ownership trail is lost and accounts become orphaned.

SEC-SQL-AU-006-RC15.name: Remediation effort underestimated
SEC-SQL-AU-006-RC15.desc: Removing dormant accounts is deferred due to fear of breaking "hidden" dependencies, so accounts remain enabled indefinitely.

SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC06.name: Incomplete hardening documentation
SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC06.desc: Organizations implementing database security guidance focus on external access controls but overlook local authentication; permissive local authentication rules are never hardened.

SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC08.name: No security scanning of pg_hba.conf
SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC08.desc: Deployment validation tools don't check for `trust` entries or alert administrators to the risk.

SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC13.name: Documentation templates outdated
SEC-SQL-AU-007-RC13.desc: Organization-internal database deployment guides copy old documentation that includes permissive authentication rules without explaining the risk or suggesting removal.

SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC12.name: Audit process crash
SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC12.desc: The specific background process or thread responsible for writing audit buffers to disk has crashed or stalled, stopping log generation while the DB remains active.

SEC-SQL-AUD-004-RC05.name: Log sampling/Throttling
SEC-SQL-AUD-004-RC05.desc: High-volume logging configurations may enable "sampling" (e.g., log 1 in 100 events) or "throttling" to save performance, causing failed login bursts to be missed.

SEC-SQL-AUD-004-RC06.name: Misinterpreted Error Codes
SEC-SQL-AUD-004-RC06.desc: The auditing system relies on regex parsing and fails to recognize specific vendor error codes (e.g., ORA-01017) as login failures.

SEC-SQL-AUD-004-RC08.name: Application-side suppression
SEC-SQL-AUD-004-RC08.desc: Middleware or connection poolers catch login exceptions and retry silently without the database ever logging a distinct "failure" event for each retry.

SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC06.name: Temporary Table Exclusion
SEC-SQL-AUD-005-RC06.desc: The system is configured to ignore DDL on temporary tables, but the filter is too broad and ignores real table changes.

SEC-SQL-AZ-001-RC03.name: Developer environments influence production practices
SEC-SQL-AZ-001-RC03.desc: Developers working in development/test environments with elevated permissions (such as db_owner or DBA) write code assuming those privileges, then request the same elevated access in production to avoid refactoring.

SEC-SQL-AZ-003-RC02.name: Manual offboarding processes with gaps
SEC-SQL-AZ-003-RC02.desc: Exit procedures exist but are incomplete, error-prone, or not followed consistently; database account deprovisioning is often overlooked while network and application access are revoked.

SEC-SQL-AZ-001-RC04.name: Time pressure and perceived operational convenience
SEC-SQL-AZ-001-RC04.desc: DBAs and administrators grant DBA or superuser roles to satisfy urgent requests faster than identifying and granting specific required privileges, treating elevated access as a shortcut to enable functionality.

SEC-SQL-AZ-001-RC05.name: Inadequate permission analysis during application deployment
SEC-SQL-AZ-001-RC05.desc: Developers and application teams fail to precisely determine which privileges are needed during deployment scripting, instead requesting broad administrative rights to ensure "everything works."

SEC-SQL-AZ-001-RC07.name: Third-party application vendor requirements
SEC-SQL-AZ-001-RC07.desc: ISVs and third-party software vendors explicitly require or recommend DBA-level privileges for their applications, and organizations grant these without evaluating the actual necessity.

SEC-SQL-AZ-001-RC10.name: Legacy applications with hardcoded privilege assumptions
SEC-SQL-AZ-001-RC10.desc: Older applications were built assuming superuser-level database access; refactoring these to use constrained permissions is expensive, so elevated access persists.

SEC-SQL-AZ-001-RC11.name: Knowledge gaps and lack of training
SEC-SQL-AZ-001-RC11.desc: DBAs, application teams, and management lack education about the principle of least privilege, security risks of excessive permissions, and techniques for granular access control.

SEC-SQL-AZ-002-RC03.name: Temporary workarounds becoming permanent
SEC-SQL-AZ-002-RC03.desc: Initial troubleshooting grants to rootcause are intended as temporary solutions but remain in place permanently once the immediate issue is resolved.

SEC-SQL-AZ-002-RC12.name: Tool or vendor recommendations that are unsafe
SEC-SQL-AZ-002-RC12.desc: Third-party tools or vendors recommend granting specific permissions to rootcause as the simplest configuration approach.

SEC-SQL-AZ-002-RC13.name: Emergency access during incidents
SEC-SQL-AZ-002-RC13.desc: During production outages or incidents, rootcause permissions are temporarily granted to enable rapid troubleshooting; these are never revoked once normalcy is restored.

SEC-SQL-AZ-003-RC03.name: Delayed or forgotten deprovisioning
SEC-SQL-AZ-003-RC03.desc: Deprovisioning requests are submitted but not executed in a timely manner, particularly during periods of high staff turnover or when the DBA handling the request leaves without completing it.

SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC04.name: No approval workflow for permission delegation
SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC04.desc: Users with WITH GRANT OPTION can grant privileges to other users without any review, audit, or approval process; unvetted privilege escalations occur freely.

SEC-SQL-AZ-003-RC12.name: Lack of privileged access management (PAM) systems
SEC-SQL-AZ-003-RC12.desc: Without centralized privileged account management, individual DBAs manage credentials and account lifecycles inconsistently.

SEC-SQL-AZ-003-RC14.name: Failed or incomplete migration processes
SEC-SQL-AZ-003-RC14.desc: During database migrations or major system changes, legacy accounts are migrated along with data; documentation of why they are needed is lost.

SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC13.name: Privilege grants during emergency scenarios
SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC13.desc: During incident response or data recovery situations, FILE privileges are temporarily granted; they are not revoked after the emergency passes.

SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC14.name: Misunderstanding of attack vectors
SEC-SQL-AZ-004-RC14.desc: Administrators do not fully appreciate that FILE privilege allows attackers to overwrite system files, load malicious libraries, or exfiltrate sensitive OS files (e.g., /etc/passwd).

SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC01.name: Insufficient understanding of ownership chaining mechanics
SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC01.desc: Database architects and administrators do not fully understand how ownership chaining bypasses permission checks across databases; they enable the feature without recognizing the security implications.

SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC02.name: Convenience over security principle
SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC02.desc: Cross-database ownership chaining simplifies permission management by allowing stored procedures to access objects in other databases without explicit permission grants; this operational convenience outweighs security concerns.

SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC12.name: Compliance framework gaps
SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC12.desc: Organizations lack policies or controls aligned with frameworks (SOX, HIPAA, ISO 27001) that restrict the ability to delegate privileges.

SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC03.name: Legacy application design assuming ownership chaining
SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC03.desc: Older applications were architected with the assumption that ownership chaining would be enabled; disabling it would require application refactoring, so the setting remains enabled.

SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC04.name: Unclear ownership across multiple databases
SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC04.desc: When database ownership is complex (different owners across different databases, or ownership changes over time), administrators enable cross-database chaining to simplify the permission model rather than clarifying and rationalizing ownership.

SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC03.name: .NET Framework Constraints
SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC03.desc: Applications use .NET Framework versions prior to 4.6 which do not natively support TLS 1.2. Applications cannot be upgraded due to Windows OS version limitations or vendor support requirements.

SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC05.name: Multi-database applications without explicit permission architecture
SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC05.desc: Applications that legitimately access multiple databases across a server do not implement explicit cross-database permissions; instead, ownership chaining is relied upon.

SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC14.name: Confusion between intent and capability
SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC14.desc: Administrators may not realize that granting a privilege WITH GRANT OPTION to a low-privilege user is a security risk; they assume the low-privilege user will not abuse the capability.

SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC06.name: Migration from single-database to multi-database environments
SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC06.desc: Organizations originally designed for a single database later expand to multiple databases; rather than redesigning permission structures, cross-database chaining is enabled to preserve existing privilege logic.

SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC08.name: Lack of audit or monitoring of cross-database access
SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC08.desc: No logging or alerting occurs when a stored procedure in one database accesses objects in another; unintended privilege escalations are not detected.

SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC09.name: Testing configurations carried forward to production
SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC09.desc: Test or development environments enable cross-database chaining for convenience; these settings are replicated to production without review.

SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC10.name: Third-party vendor requirements or recommendations
SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC10.desc: ERP, CRM, or other enterprise applications require or recommend enabling cross-database chaining; organizations enable it at the server level to support multiple vendor applications.

SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC11.name: Incomplete understanding of risk when owner differs
SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC11.desc: Administrators may not realize that cross-database chaining only forms if both databases are owned by the same login; when this condition is met (often unintentionally), privilege escalation becomes possible.

SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC12.name: Database isolation principle not enforced
SEC-SQL-AZ-005-RC12.desc: Organizations lack a architectural principle that databases should be isolated from each other; without this principle, cross-database access is seen as acceptable.

SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC02.name: Inadequate understanding of WITH GRANT OPTION implications
SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC02.desc: Administrators and users do not fully understand that WITH GRANT OPTION allows privilege escalation; they view it simply as "letting users grant other users access" without recognizing the security risks.

SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC11.name: Implicit grant options in template scripts
SEC-SQL-AZ-006-RC11.desc: Database provisioning scripts or configuration templates include WITH GRANT OPTION in GRANT statements; these are copied across multiple databases without review.

SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC08.name: Registry Modification
SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC08.desc: CLR code can modify Windows registry; attacker can alter system configuration, disable antivirus, or create persistence mechanisms

SEC-SQL-CFG-002-RC10.name: Client-Side Exploitation
SEC-SQL-CFG-002-RC10.desc: Man-in-the-middle or compromised client application can trigger unsolicited LOAD DATA LOCAL requests to read server-side files from client perspective

SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC04.name: Migration Process Gaps
SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC04.desc: Database migration tools (like Microsoft Data Migration Assistant) transfer all objects including test schemas; migrators don't filter schemas by importance

SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC05.name: Knowledge Loss During Transitions
SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC05.desc: Original DBA/team that provisioned environment leaves organization; new team unaware of which databases are legitimate vs. test artifacts

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC03.name: rootcause Database Link Exposure
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC03.desc: Link created as rootcause rather than private; all database users inherit ability to use link rather than restricted set

SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC06.name: Inadequate Cleanup Procedures
SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC06.desc: Post-deployment scripts don't include cleanup steps to remove sample databases after server is hardened

SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC11.name: Compliance Scope Confusion
SEC-SQL-CFG-003-RC11.desc: Assumption that test/sample databases are exempt from data protection policies; sample data treated casually despite containing realistic PII from examples

SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC01.name: Application Code Execution Requirement
SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC01.desc: Applications written with managed code routines deployed as CLR assemblies; feature enabled to support this architecture

SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC03.name: Third-Party Tool Dependencies
SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC03.desc: SSISDB (Integration Services), Reporting Services, or replication features require CLR to function; enabling CLR is collateral consequence

SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC04.name: Unsigned Assembly Bypass
SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC04.desc: CLR strict security disabled to avoid certificate signing requirements on assemblies; enabled feature persists even if original assemblies removed

SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC05.name: Lack of Assembly Vetting
SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC05.desc: CLR assemblies deployed without security review; code review process doesn't identify untrusted or overprivileged operations

SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC06.name: Privilege Escalation via CLR
SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC06.desc: Attacker with limited database privileges creates malicious CLR assembly to execute with database engine's process privileges (often highly elevated)

SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC07.name: Sandbox Escape
SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC07.desc: CLR "safe" assemblies contain vulnerabilities allowing escape from .NET sandbox; enables file system access or process execution despite SAFE designation

SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC04.name: Java/JDK Version Limitations
SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC04.desc: Older Java applications run on JDK versions that do not support TLS 1.2+ without additional configuration or patches that the organization has not applied.

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC04.name: Privilege Escalation via Link
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC04.desc: Low-privilege user on local database (read-only access) discovers rootcause link to remote database with high privileges; escalates access cross-database

SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC09.name: Network-Based Attacks
SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC09.desc: CLR assemblies can initiate arbitrary network connections (if written poorly) to exfiltrate data or download additional payloads

SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC10.name: External Library Access
SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC10.desc: CLR code can load additional .NET libraries that provide unrestricted OS access, bypassing intended security boundaries

SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC11.name: Post-Exploitation Persistence
SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC11.desc: Once CLR enabled, attacker can create malicious procedure to persist access across restarts; difficult to detect without assembly auditing

SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC12.name: Insufficient Configuration Segregation
SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC12.desc: Trustworthy flag or CLR strict security configured at instance level; affects all databases despite only one or two needing the feature

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC08.name: Remote Database Exploitation
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC08.desc: Compromised local database account uses link to compromise remote database; removes network boundary to breach remote systems

SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC13.name: Monitoring Gaps
SEC-SQL-CFG-004-RC13.desc: No alerting on CLR assembly creation or execution; malicious CLR activity remains undetected

SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC09.name: Undocumented Server Requirements
SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC09.desc: Third-party application silently depends on particular trace flag being enabled; application breaks if flag removed despite original need unclear

SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC14.name: Misunderstanding Hidden Features
SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC14.desc: DBA confuses trace flags with standard configuration parameters; treats trace flags as permanent settings rather than debugging tools

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC01.name: Static Credential Storage
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC01.desc: Database links configured with fixed usernames/passwords stored unencrypted in link definition; attacker with read access to data dictionary views can extract credentials

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC02.name: Overprivileged Link Credentials
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC02.desc: Link configured to connect as highly privileged user (DBA, admin role) to remote database; anyone accessing the local database can implicitly access remote database as admin

SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC10.name: Lack of Security Requirements
SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC10.desc: No security policy or compliance mandate exists requiring encrypted connections. Encryption is treated as optional rather than mandatory.

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC05.name: Inadequate Access Control
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC05.desc: No validation in link definition that local users with access to link should have equivalent privileges on remote database

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC06.name: Cross-Database Privilege Inheritance
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC06.desc: Assumption that local database privilege restrictions apply to remote database; actually grants unrestricted access to remote tables within remote user's privileges

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC07.name: Unvalidated Dynamic Queries
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC07.desc: Link used in dynamic SQL or application code without parameterization; allows SQL injection through database link to execute arbitrary remote commands

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC09.name: Credential Exposure via Monitoring
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC09.desc: Link credentials visible in database alert logs, monitoring tools, or query plans; exposed through overly permissive system catalog access

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC10.name: Long-Lived Credentials
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC10.desc: Link credentials never rotated; if exposed in any context (decommissioned server, backup leak), attacker has permanent access

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC11.name: Scope Confusion
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC11.desc: Organization unaware that link credential applies across all schemas/users; assumes capability is restricted to specific applications

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC12.name: Network Segmentation Bypass
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC12.desc: Application-layer network controls don't apply to database links; link bypasses firewall rules between database tiers

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC13.name: Linked Server Configuration Persistence
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC13.desc: Database links configured during migration or initial setup, persists even after application requirements change

SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC14.name: Competing Priorities in Development Cycles
SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC14.desc: Encryption configuration is deprioritized in favor of feature delivery and bug fixes during development sprints.

SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC07.name: Load Balancer and Infrastructure TLS Settings
SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC07.desc: Network load balancers, firewalls, or proxies between clients and databases are configured to allow TLS 1.0/1.1 for "compatibility," and the database inherits these weaker settings.

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC14.name: Missing Encryption
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC14.desc: Link credentials transmitted unencrypted over network; exposed to any network sniffer between databases (especially in cloud/shared networks)

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC15.name: Mutual Authentication Gaps
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC15.desc: Links don't validate remote database identity; susceptible to man-in-the-middle attacks where attacker masquerades as remote database

SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC16.name: Catalog-Level Exposure
SEC-SQL-CFG-006-RC16.desc: Data dictionary views exposing link connection strings to users who need only the functional capability (not configuration details)

SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC05.name: Cost and Performance Concerns
SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC05.desc: Organizations avoid encryption due to perceived CPU overhead (typically 5-10% per source) and the cost of hardware upgrades or HSM integration, without proper ROI analysis.
