SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC06.name: Lack of DBA Encryption Knowledge
SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC06.desc: Database administrators lack the expertise to properly configure TLS/SSL certificates, manage certificate lifecycles, or troubleshoot encryption-related issues. They avoid implementing encryption to prevent breaking production systems.

SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC09.name: Network Architecture Assumptions
SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC09.desc: Teams assume database communication occurs only on trusted internal networks (VLANs, firewalls) and therefore believe encryption is unnecessary, missing VLAN hopping, rogue access point, and internal threat vectors.

SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC08.name: Lack of TLS 1.2 Configuration Knowledge
SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC08.desc: DBAs do not know how to properly configure TLS 1.2 as the minimum version without breaking existing applications and choose to leave weaker versions enabled as a workaround.

SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC10.name: Intentional Compatibility Decisions
SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC10.desc: Organizations made an explicit decision to support legacy clients for business reasons (customer contracts, managed service agreements) without implementing compensating controls.

SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC14.name: Vendor Testing Incompleteness
SEC-SQL-ENC-002-RC14.desc: The organization tested upgrading to TLS 1.2-only with a small subset of applications but did not complete organization-wide testing, leaving legacy protocols enabled pending full migration.

SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC03.name: Missing License Entitlements
SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC03.desc: Organizations own licenses but they were not provisioned or activated in the license management system, so TDE activation is blocked.

SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC09.name: Administrative Overhead
SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC09.desc: DBAs perceive TDE as requiring extensive configuration, monitoring, and key rotation processes that they are not equipped to manage.

SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC13.name: Development/Test Database Assumption
SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC13.desc: Organizations assume TDE is only needed in production and do not enable it in development databases, then never backfill to production due to risk aversion.

SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC14.name: Lack of Compliance Driver
SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC14.desc: The organization operates in a vertical without strict data protection regulations (e.g., not HIPAA, PCI-DSS, GDPR-governed), so there is no compliance mandate to encrypt data at rest.

SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC15.name: Previous Failed Implementation Attempt
SEC-SQL-ENC-003-RC15.desc: An earlier attempt to enable TDE caused unexpected downtime or performance degradation, and the organization has not attempted it since.

SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC02.name: Backup Software Doesn't Support Encryption
SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC02.desc: Legacy backup software (Veritas, CommVault, or in-house scripts) does not support database backup encryption or was configured before encryption features were added.

SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC06.name: Backup Storage Assumptions
SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC06.desc: Backups are stored in what the organization considers secure locations (isolated networks, locked rooms) and the team assumes backups do not need encryption because physical access is restricted.

SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC07.name: Regulatory Requirement Not Mapped to Backups
SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC07.desc: Compliance policies (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS) require data encryption but the organization interprets this as applying only to the live database, not backup files.

SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC08.name: Off-Site Backup Storage Not Recognized as High Risk
SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC08.desc: Backups sent to cloud storage or third-party sites are not encrypted, even though this increases exposure. The organization assumes the third party's security is sufficient.

SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC09.name: Backup Recovery Testing Not Performed
SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC09.desc: Encryption was never tested end-to-end because the organization does not regularly test backup recovery. When tested, it failed due to missing keys or incompatible encryption formats.

SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC13.name: Multiple Backup Destinations Not Coordinated
SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC13.desc: Backups are taken to local storage, network shares, and cloud storage with different tools and configurations. Some destinations support encryption, others do not, and the organization defaults to no encryption for consistency.

SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC14.name: Backup Retention Policy Overrides Encryption
SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC14.desc: Backup retention policies store backups for years (regulatory requirement), and encrypting older backups is seen as too complex. The organization keeps backups unencrypted to simplify management.

SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC15.name: Developer and QA Databases Using Production Backups
SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC15.desc: Unencrypted backup files are regularly restored to development and QA environments for testing, and the organization fears encryption will complicate this workflow.

SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC16.name: Backup Scripts Written Before Encryption Features Existed
SEC-SQL-ENC-004-RC16.desc: In-house backup scripts were written years ago and have not been updated despite new encryption capabilities in the database platform.

SEC-SQL-ENC-005-RC06.name: Key Generation with Insufficient Entropy
SEC-SQL-ENC-005-RC06.desc: Encryption keys or certificates were generated in a way that resulted in weak key material (e.g., Debian weak key generation vulnerability, keys generated from predictable seeds).

SEC-SQL-ENC-005-RC15.name: Compliance Requirements Misunderstood
SEC-SQL-ENC-005-RC15.desc: PCI-DSS, HIPAA, and other standards specify "strong encryption" but do not define exact algorithms or key lengths. Organizations interpret this loosely and use weaker algorithms they believe still meet "strong" criteria.

SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC03.name: Lack of awareness and training
SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC03.desc: Nearly one-third of developers lack familiarity with secure coding practices; developers may not understand how SQL injection works or the risks of dynamic SQL without proper safeguards.

SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC05.name: Time pressure and deadline constraints
SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC05.desc: Development teams under strict deadlines resort to shortcuts using simple string concatenation rather than implementing proper parameterized queries, which require more upfront effort.

SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC06.name: Insufficient security code reviews
SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC06.desc: Code review processes may not specifically check for SQL injection vulnerabilities or dynamic SQL patterns; reviewers may lack security expertise or prioritize functionality over security.

SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC10.name: ORM framework misuse
SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC10.desc: Developers bypass ORM safety features by using raw SQL methods with string interpolation instead of the framework's parameterized query builders (e.g., FromSqlRaw, raw SQL in Hibernate/JPA without parameter binding).

SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC11.name: Absence of security testing tools
SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC11.desc: No static code analysis, SAST tools, or runtime detection mechanisms in place to identify dynamic SQL patterns before production deployment.

SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC12.name: Third-party library dependencies
SEC-SQL-INJ-001-RC12.desc: Application relies on vendor code, legacy libraries, or abstraction layers that generate SQL dynamically; developers have limited visibility into actual SQL being constructed at runtime.

SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC09.name: Assumption of network isolation
SEC-SQL-INJ-002-RC09.desc: False belief that database servers are sufficiently isolated from threats; assumption that only trusted internal users can execute SQL injection attacks against database.

SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC03.name: rootcause Cloud Instance Configuration
SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC03.desc: Cloud-managed databases (AWS RDS, Azure Database, Google Cloud SQL) explicitly configured with "rootcause Access" or "rootcausely Accessible" enabled when this should be restricted to private VPC/VNet access.

SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC04.name: Inadequate Network Segmentation
SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC04.desc: No isolated network zones or VLANs separating database servers from rootcause-facing infrastructure. Flat network architecture treats all systems as equally accessible.

SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC06.name: Disabled or Absent Firewall Rules
SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC06.desc: Host-level or network-level firewalls either disabled entirely or configured with permissive default-allow policies rather than default-deny.

SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC07.name: Missing Virtual Private Network (VPN) Requirements
SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC07.desc: No requirement for clients to connect through VPN before accessing database. Database directly exposed without intermediary access controls.

SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC08.name: Cloud Provider Shared Responsibility Model Misunderstanding
SEC-SQL-NET-001-RC08.desc: Developers assume the cloud provider has secured all database access by default, not realizing they must explicitly restrict rootcause accessibility.

SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC10.name: Assumption Port Numbers Alone Provide Security
SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC10.desc: Administrators mistakenly believe that firewalls will block external access regardless of port number used, underestimating the impact of default port predictability.

SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC11.name: No Centralized Port Management
SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC11.desc: Organizations lack enterprise-wide port allocation standards, allowing ad-hoc default port usage across departments.

SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC06.name: Package Manager and Repository Access
SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC06.desc: Database software accessing package repositories, pip/npm registries, or cloud storage for libraries and dependencies. No restrictions on destination servers or protocols.

SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC07.name: No Network Policy Enforcement at OS Level
SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC07.desc: Linux/Unix servers running databases without iptables/firewalld rules. Windows servers without Windows Firewall outbound rules.

SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC08.name: Cloud Provider NAT Gateway Configuration
SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC08.desc: AWS/Azure/GCP configured to provide internet access to database instances without explicit routing restrictions. Default behavior allows all outbound traffic.

SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC09.name: Lack of Web Proxy or Firewall Mediation
SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC09.desc: No proxy or firewall appliance between database and internet. Direct routing enabled for all protocols and destinations.

SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC11.name: No Segmented Database Network Zone
SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC11.desc: Database in the same network segment as application servers, which require internet access for updates/APIs. Segmentation controls too permissive.

SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC12.name: Legacy System Requirements
SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC12.desc: Older databases or dependent applications required direct internet access for licensing, callbacks, or legacy protocol support. Continued even after modernization.

SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC13.name: Configuration Management Tool Access
SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC13.desc: Databases with access to configuration management systems (Puppet, Ansible) that require internet connectivity. No restrictions on which external systems can communicate.

SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC16.name: No Default-Deny Egress Policy
SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC16.desc: Organizations didn't implement zero-trust outbound policies. Standard practice is to allow unless explicitly denied.

SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC17.name: Lack of Connection State Inspection
SEC-SQL-NET-003-RC17.desc: Firewalls not configured for stateful inspection of outbound connections. Allow rules too permissive on protocols and ports.

SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC03.name: High perceived costs of planned upgrades
SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC03.desc: Organizations prioritize short-term budget constraints over long-term risk mitigation, viewing upgrade expenses as capital expenditures rather than security investments.

SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC04.name: Extended downtime requirements for migration
SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC04.desc: Organizations operating 24/7 systems fear the substantial downtime needed for major version migrations, particularly when zero-downtime solutions are unavailable or prohibitively complex to implement.

SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC06.name: Unfamiliar upgrade procedures and architectural changes
SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC06.desc: Teams lack expertise or documented procedures for their specific database engine and environment, creating fear of failed migrations or unexpected compatibility issues.

SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC07.name: Inadequate testing environments that mimic production
SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC07.desc: Organizations cannot afford or maintain staging environments with representative data volumes and configurations, making safe upgrade testing impossible.

SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC03.name: Performance Overhead Fears
SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC03.desc: Developers avoid column-level encryption due to fears that decryption overhead will slow down high-throughput queries or increase CPU usage significantly.

SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC07.name: ETL \& Data Warehousing Stripping
SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC07.desc: While the transactional database might encrypt sensitive columns, the ETL process that moves data to an analytics warehouse often decrypts it to simplify analyst queries, leaving the warehouse copy exposed.

SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC01.name: Inadequate separation of MC configuration and database privileges
SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC01.desc: MC users have dual privilege layers (configuration roles and database access) that can be misaligned, allowing users to retain excessive access in one layer while appearing restricted in another

SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC02.name: Improper user mapping between MC accounts and database users
SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC02.desc: When MC users are mapped to overly privileged database accounts (like dbadmin), they inherit dangerous capabilities that bypass MC's intended restrictions

SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC03.name: Overly permissive default role assignments
SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC03.desc: MC's predefined roles (Admin, Associate, IT, User) often grant broader privileges than necessary, violating least privilege principles by default

SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC05.name: Lack of regular privilege audits
SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC05.desc: Organizations fail to periodically review MC user assignments, mapped database accounts, and inherited privileges, allowing drift toward excessive access

SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC06.name: Insufficient training on dual privilege model
SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC06.desc: Database administrators may not understand how MC privileges interact with database-level grants, leading to misconfigurations

SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC07.name: Shared MC administrator accounts
SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC07.desc: Multiple users sharing the MC SUPER administrator account eliminates individual accountability and makes it impossible to enforce role-based access

SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC08.name: Stale user accounts retaining privileges
SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC08.desc: Former employees or transferred users often retain MC access and database mappings long after their legitimate need expires

SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC09.name: Inadequate privilege documentation
SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC09.desc: Lack of clear documentation on which MC privileges are required for specific job functions leads to over-provisioning

SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC10.name: No automated monitoring for privilege changes
SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC10.desc: Absence of alerting when MC users are granted new roles or mapped to different database accounts prevents timely detection of policy violations

SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC11.name: Inheritance of excessive privileges from mapped accounts
SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC11.desc: MC users mapped to database accounts with DBA or pseudosuperuser roles gain unrestricted access regardless of MC role assignments

SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC12.name: Use of default administrative credentials
SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC12.desc: Failure to change default MC SUPER administrator passwords creates a critical single point of failure

SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC13.name: Insufficient testing of privilege configurations
SEC-SQL-VS-001-RC13.desc: Organizations deploy MC privilege structures without validating that they enforce intended restrictions in practice

SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC05.name: Memory-only logging
SEC-SQL-AUD-002-RC05.desc: Auditing is configured to write to a memory buffer (ring buffer) which is lost upon database restart or when the buffer wraps around.

SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC07.name: Non-repudiation features disabled
SEC-SQL-AUD-003-RC07.desc: Cryptographic signing or chaining of audit records (where supported) is disabled, allowing modification of middle records without breaking a chain.

SEC-SQL-AUD-007-RC05.name: Execution of previously unseen stored procedures or functions
SEC-SQL-AUD-007-RC05.desc: A stored procedure or function that has never appeared in historical workload logs is called, potentially indicating a backdoor or newly injected code object.

SEC-SQL-AUD-008-RC01.name: Bulk data export or mass SELECT on sensitive tables
SEC-SQL-AUD-008-RC01.desc: A single session issues SELECT queries returning unusually large row counts from tables classified as sensitive, consistent with data exfiltration.

SEC-SQL-AU-001-RC01.name: Installation defaults not changed
SEC-SQL-AU-001-RC01.desc: Database installation scripts create superuser/admin accounts with known names by default. Administrators forget or skip the post-installation hardening step to rename, disable, or change credentials.

SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC01.name: Global logging switch is disabled
SEC-SQL-AUD-001-RC01.desc: The master configuration parameter controlling all logging (e.g., `logging_collector`, `general_log`) is set to "off" or "0" in the primary configuration file.

SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC01.name: Default Configuration Not Changed
SEC-SQL-ENC-001-RC01.desc: Many database engines have TLS/SSL encryption disabled by default in their initial configuration files. Organizations deploy databases without reviewing and updating these defaults.

SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC01.name: Lack of proactive EOL tracking and monitoring
SEC-SQL-PAT-001-RC01.desc: Organizations fail to establish processes that monitor vendor EOL announcements, resulting in systems unknowingly drifting past support end dates without awareness or planning.

SEC-SQL-AUD-008-RC02.name: Mass DELETE or TRUNCATE without WHERE clause
SEC-SQL-AUD-008-RC02.desc: A DELETE with no predicate or a TRUNCATE statement executes against a non-empty table, risking irreversible data loss.

SEC-SQL-AZ-001-RC01.name: Lack of Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) implementation
SEC-SQL-AZ-001-RC01.desc: Organizations without mature RBAC systems grant permissions on an ad hoc basis rather than aligning them to defined job roles, resulting in superuser privileges being distributed widely across the user population.

SEC-SQL-AU-006-RC01.name: No activity monitoring
SEC-SQL-AU-006-RC01.desc: Databases lack or don't use login activity logging; dormant accounts are invisible without manual audits.

SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC01.name: Troubleshooting Discovery
SEC-SQL-CFG-005-RC01.desc: DBA encounters performance issue, reads online that trace flag X will help, enables it without full understanding of side effects

SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC01.name: Default Configuration Never Changed
SEC-SQL-NET-002-RC01.desc: Database installed with factory defaults and administrators never modified the listening port. Databases ship with well-known default ports that are easily enumerated by attackers.

SEC-SQL-AUD-008-RC03.name: DDL statements executed in production by non-DBA accounts
SEC-SQL-AUD-008-RC03.desc: CREATE, ALTER, or DROP statements are executed by accounts that do not hold an approved DBA role, violating change-management controls.

SEC-SQL-ACC-010-RC07.name: After-hours transaction activity
SEC-SQL-ACC-010-RC07.desc: Transactions are running outside normal business hours (before 06:00 or after 22:00 server local time). After-hours database activity is a common indicator of compromised credentials, insider threats, or unauthorized batch processes.

SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC16.name: All columns discovered in schema
SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC16.desc: Full inventory of every column in the database schema (all columns, not just sensitive/PII columns) - the same schema-mapping detection as SEC-SQL-PRI-001-RC12 but without the sensitive-column filter. Provides complete column coverage for data classification and schema auditing.

SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC01.name: Default Configuration
SEC-DOC-AUD-001-RC01.desc: Most database engines ship with audit logging disabled by default to minimize performance impact and disk usage.

SEC-SQL-AUD-025-RC01.name: Unauthorized data change (UPDATE/DELETE/INSERT) to designated sensitive tables detected
SEC-SQL-AUD-025-RC01.desc: Captures data-changing DML (UPDATE / DELETE / INSERT) against designated sensitive business-data tables (Flexcube customer/account PII: FSDH_CUSTOMER_BVN, STTM_Customer, STTM_Cust_Account, STTM_Personal, STTM_Corporate ...). Oracle reads V$SQL (command_type 6/7/2, plan cache); SQL Server reads dm_exec_query_stats; MySQL/MariaDB read performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest. The table list is embedded in the rule SQL - edit it to add/adjust sensitive objects. Verify by running an UPDATE against a listed table.

SEC-SQL-AUD-026-RC01.name: Unauthorized privilege escalation - account holds elevated/administrative privileges
SEC-SQL-AUD-026-RC01.desc: Detects privilege escalation by STATE: lists accounts (excluding the DBMS-maintained baseline) that currently HOLD elevated / administrative roles or privileges. Oracle reads DBA_ROLE_PRIVS + DBA_SYS_PRIVS (DBA, *_FULL_DATABASE, ALTER SYSTEM, GRANT ANY, ANY-object privileges, CREATE/ALTER/DROP USER); SQL Server reads sys.server_role_members (sysadmin/securityadmin/serveradmin/...); MySQL/MariaDB read mysql.user global privileges (SUPER, GRANT OPTION, CREATE USER, SHUTDOWN, RELOAD). State-based detection is reliable without any audit configuration and self-clears when the grant is revoked. The...

SEC-SQL-ACC-030-RC01.name: Applicative login used from a watched program
SEC-SQL-ACC-030-RC01.desc: An active transaction was seen whose login_name matches metrics.app_logins AND whose program_name matches metrics.programs for that server. Detected by the app_login_guard analysis process, which raises an alert and (subject to the blocker_dry_run switch) kills the offending session.

SEC-SQL-AUD-031-RC01.name: Mass in-place encryption of data (ransomware)
SEC-SQL-AUD-031-RC01.desc: A user session is overwriting data with encrypted/binary values (ENCRYPTBYKEY/PASSPHRASE/CERT or large 0x blobs in UPDATE statements) - the signature of in-place ransomware encryption.

SEC-SQL-AUD-031-RC02.name: Mass data-modification velocity (ransomware sweep)
SEC-SQL-AUD-031-RC02.desc: A single login is issuing an abnormally high number of data-modification statements in a short window (config.global_params ransomware_mod_velocity) - a ransomware encryption sweep across the schema.

SEC-SQL-AUD-031-RC03.name: Ransom-note artifacts detected
SEC-SQL-AUD-031-RC03.desc: Active transaction SQL contains ransom-note indicators (e.g. "your files are encrypted", decrypt/bitcoin/.onion, readme/recover objects) - attacker leaving payment instructions.

SEC-SQL-AUD-031-RC04.name: Bulk export followed by mass delete (double-extortion)
SEC-SQL-AUD-031-RC04.desc: A single login both exfiltrated data (bulk export: SELECT INTO / bcp / OPENROWSET / SELECT *) and destroyed data (TRUNCATE / DROP / DELETE without WHERE) within the same window - the double-extortion ransomware pattern.

SEC-SQL-AUD-031-RC05.name: System command / OLE automation from a session (ransomware delivery)
SEC-SQL-AUD-031-RC05.desc: A session invoked OS command / external process capabilities (xp_cmdshell, sp_OACreate/sp_OAMethod, xp_dirtree, sp_execute_external_script, BULK INSERT / OPENROWSET(BULK), xp_regwrite) - the delivery/execution mechanism for ransomware and exfiltration.

SEC-SQL-AUD-027-RC01.name: Destructive operation attempted - DROP/TRUNCATE/BACKUP command detected (including failed attempts)
SEC-SQL-AUD-027-RC01.desc: Detects destructive command activity across ALL databases of the monitored instance: DROP TABLE, DROP DATABASE/SCHEMA, DROP LOGIN, DROP USER, DROP ROLE, TRUNCATE and BACKUP/RESTORE DATABASE (a backup taken by an attacker is data exfiltration). Failed attempts are included where the platform records them: SQL Server default-trace security-audit events carry Success=0 for denied drops of logins/users/roles; Oracle UNIFIED_AUDIT_TRAIL rows with return_code<>0 are failed attempts; MySQL/MariaDB performance_schema digests report SUM_ERRORS>0. Sources: SQL Server default trace (always on; tempdb...

SEC-DOC-AUTH-001-RC01.name: Vendor-supplied defaults remain unchanged
SEC-DOC-AUTH-001-RC01.desc: Default credentials like "admin/admin" are well-documented and rootcausely known, making them prime targets for attackers

SEC-DOC-AUTH-002-RC04.name: Legacy compatibility concerns
SEC-DOC-AUTH-002-RC04.desc: Organizations avoid strict policies to maintain compatibility with older applications

SEC-DOC-AUTH-003-RC01.name: Default CouchDB installation enables Admin Party
SEC-DOC-AUTH-003-RC01.desc: All users have administrative access without authentication by design

SEC-DOC-AUTH-004-RC01.name: Default installation without authentication
SEC-DOC-AUTH-004-RC01.desc: Older or default installations shipped with authentication disabled, allowing unauthenticated access out of the box.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC01.name: Principle of Least Privilege Not Applied
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-001-RC01.desc: Users assigned broad roles (e.g., `readWriteAnyDatabase`) to simplify initial deployment rather than granular roles with specific permissions needed for their function.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC01.name: RBAC Not Enabled by Default
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-002-RC01.desc: Many document databases ship with authentication optional and RBAC disabled; organizations proceed with default configuration assuming basic security is sufficient.

SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC01.name: Initial Development Using Admin Credentials
SEC-DOC-AUTHZ-005-RC01.desc: Applications built and tested with admin/root account for simplicity; never transitioned to lower-privilege credentials in production.

SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC01.name: Default configuration never changed
SEC-DOC-ENC-001-RC01.desc: Document databases often ship with TLS disabled by default to simplify initial setup and testing, and administrators fail to enable it for production

SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC01.name: Not enabled by default in many editions
SEC-DOC-ENC-003-RC01.desc: Community/free editions often lack encryption at rest capability entirely

SEC-DOC-INJ-003-RC02.name: JavaScript execution enabled in MongoDB configuration

SEC-DOC-NET-002-RC01.name: Lazy Configuration
SEC-DOC-NET-002-RC01.desc: Using `bindIp: 0.0.0.0` or `bindIpAll: true` is easier than listing specific private interface IPs (e.g., `10.0.1.5`).

SEC-DOC-AUD-003-RC01.name: Default Rotation Settings
SEC-DOC-AUD-003-RC01.desc: The database default log rotation is based on size (e.g., 100MB) rather than time, causing rapid deletion during high traffic.

SEC-DOC-AUTH-005-RC01.name: No rate limiting configured on authentication endpoints
SEC-DOC-AUTH-005-RC01.desc: System allows unlimited authentication attempts without throttling

SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC01.name: Default session timeout values never changed
SEC-DOC-AUTH-010-RC01.desc: Vendor defaults often excessively long for convenience over security

SEC-DOC-DAT-001-RC01.name: Lack of encryption at rest implementation
SEC-DOC-DAT-001-RC01.desc: Database encryption not enabled in configuration

SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC01.name: Legacy TLS version support for backward compatibility
SEC-DOC-ENC-002-RC01.desc: Systems configured to support TLS 1.0/1.1 to accommodate older clients or applications

SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC01.name: Lack of certificate expiry monitoring
SEC-DOC-ENC-005-RC01.desc: No automated alerting before certificates expire

SEC-DOC-NET-001-RC01.name: Misunderstood "0.0.0.0"
SEC-DOC-NET-001-RC01.desc: Administrators interpret `0.0.0.0/0` as "standard network enabling" rather than "everyone on the internet."

SEC-SQL-AUD-011-RC06.name: Unauthorised INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or DROP statement executed by a login
SEC-SQL-AUD-011-RC06.desc: A login executed a statement it is not authorised to run under metrics.login_authorizations. White rules make the ticked operations the only permitted ones; black rules forbid the ticked operations outright. Derived from the SEC-SQL-ACC-011-RC02 collected sessions by monitoring.derive_sec_sql_aud_011_rc06(), which clones the record under this metric name carrying only the unauthorised statements. Unauthorised write or DDL activity of this kind is how audit and log tables get altered or destroyed, so it is treated as critical.

SEC-VEC-ACC-001-RC01.name: Default Namespace Not Specified in Queries
SEC-VEC-ACC-001-RC01.desc: When queries omit namespace/partition parameters, systems default to global or cross-namespace result sets if default access controls are permissive

SEC-VEC-ACC-002-RC01.name: Principle of Least Privilege Not Applied During Setup
SEC-VEC-ACC-002-RC01.desc: API key generated with default admin/full access permissions; developer didn't explicitly scope down to required operations

SEC-VEC-ATK-003-RC01.name: Unbounded vector dimension acceptance
SEC-VEC-ATK-003-RC01.desc: Vector databases accept vectors of arbitrary dimensionality without limiting maximum size.

SEC-VEC-AUTH-001-RC01.name: Hardcoded credentials in source code
SEC-VEC-AUTH-001-RC01.desc: API keys embedded directly in application code, configuration files, or initialization scripts. These remain exploitable even after removal from version control history.

SEC-VEC-AUTH-003-RC01.name: TLS not enabled in configuration
SEC-VEC-AUTH-003-RC01.desc: TLS/SSL completely disabled in default configuration files; requires explicit enablement by administrator.

SEC-VEC-NET-001-RC01.name: Default binding to all interfaces
SEC-VEC-NET-001-RC01.desc: Database service binds to all network interfaces (0.0.0.0) by default. When not explicitly restricted in configuration, the service becomes rootcausely accessible on all network interfaces.

SEC-VEC-NET-002-RC01.name: insecureSkipVerify flag enabled in SDKs
SEC-VEC-NET-002-RC01.desc: Python requests.packages.urllib3.connectionpool.HTTPSConnectionPool(verify=False); Go http.Client with InsecureSkipVerify: true; Node.js with rejectUnauthorized: false

SEC-SQL-ACC-040-RC01.name: Destructive operation chain by a single login
SEC-SQL-ACC-040-RC01.desc: Four or more distinct destructive operation classes (mass update, mass delete, drop, truncate, backup tampering, audit disable, shell/bulk, privilege grant) were observed from one login on one server within a few minutes. Individually these can be legitimate; in a short chain they are the ransomware signature. Scheduled archive and maintenance jobs produce a similar shape, which is what the security agent triages.
